articles.title: I’m a Philly forensic psychologist who has conducted dozens of psychopathic evaluations – here’s why an evaluation of R.C. Horsch in the ‘80s didn’t identify him as a possible psychopath
articles.author: David DeMatteo, Professor of Law and Psychology, Drexel University
paras: Seven missing women have been linked to the house that was shared by 44-year-old Eugene Horsch and his late father, Raymond “R.C.” Horsch, in the Olney section of Philadelphia.

With five of the seven women feared dead, Philadelphia police and the FBI are conducting a massive investigation of the home. Law enforcement has said Raymond Horsch, who died in 2025 at the age of 82, is the suspected killer. Eugene Horsch has not been charged with any homicides or missing-person offenses related to the missing women.

The Horsch house investigation raises questions about serial killers and whether mental health professionals can identify a person at risk of becoming one. The early identification of psychopathy can potentially prevent an escalation of antisocial behavior.

As a forensic psychologist, I conduct psychological evaluations to help courts make decisions when someone’s mental health is relevant. I’ve conducted hundreds of forensic psychological evaluations, including dozens with individuals with psychopathic characteristics.

I’m not surprised that a previous psychological evaluation of R.C. Horsch, done in the mid-1980s, did not identify him as a potential psychopath. That’s because reliable tools for identifying psychopathy were not available at that time.

Psychopathic personality disorder, or psychopathy, is not an officially recognized disorder in the current version of the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM. This is the primary diagnostic resource used by mental health professionals in the United States.

Although a version of psychopathy was included in prior editions of the DSM, more recent editions have eliminated the diagnosis. This is because of the difficulty in assessing some of the emotional characteristics of psychopathy.

Instead, the DSM includes a diagnosis for antisocial personality disorder, which focuses primarily on the behavioral aspects of psychopathy. Psychopathy is generally considered to be a more extreme variant of antisocial personality disorder.
While psychopathy is no longer in the DSM, it has been vigorously researched and written about for decades.

It is characterized by a distinct group of personality, behavioral and emotional traits. It has been defined in slightly different ways over the years, but some of the traits commonly associated with psychopathy include pathological lying, extreme narcissism, shallow affect, impulsivity and lack of empathy and remorse.
Psychopathy is also characterized by a persistent pattern of antisocial or manipulative behaviors. These can range from infidelity and intimidation to aggression and extreme violence.
Psychopathy and serial killers

The link between serial killers – individuals who kill several people in separate, unrelated events over a period of time – and psychopathy is not new. Several well-known American serial killers, including Ted Bundy and Jeffrey Dahmer, are suspected to have had psychopathic personality disorder.

To be clear, most individuals with psychopathic personality disorder are not serial killers. In fact, people with psychopathic characteristics can be found among corporate executives, elected officials and attorneys.
But some traits associated with extreme psychopathy, including the ability to engage in violent behavior with little remorse or guilt, are typically found among serial killers.

Given that psychopathic characteristics are common among serial killers, one might wonder: Can mental health professionals identify psychopathy when conducting a psychological evaluation and possibly thwart a future serial killer?

Mental health professionals are frequently asked to conduct evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system who’ve been accused or convicted of serious crimes. For example, we might evaluate someone to help a court determine whether the person is competent to stand trial, or whether they should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.

Identifying whether a person has psychopathic characteristics may also be relevant to how a court sentences them after conviction. Individuals with more psychopathic characteristics typically present a higher risk for future criminal behavior. As such, because of the discretion given to judges and juries when it comes to sentencing in most states, courts are more likely to give a longer sentence because of the increased risk to public safety.
One of the most widely used psychopathy assessment tools, the psychopathy checklist-revised, or PCL-R, has been the subject of tremendous research over the past few decades.

Most studies find that the PCL-R can reliably identify psychopathic characteristics in both research and clinical settings. Individuals with higher PCL-R scores are more psychopathic and, therefore, at higher risk of engaging in future criminal behavior.

In 1985, R.C. Horsch was convicted in federal court of charges related to counterfeiting and methamphetamine manufacturing. As part of the federal sentencing proceedings, he underwent a lengthy psychological evaluation, which the Philadelphia Inquirer obtained through a federal records request.

The psychologist described Horsch as “grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious and excessively controlling,” and noted that he was “consumed by anger.” He concluded that Horsch likely had bipolar disorder and paranoid personality disorder.
The psychological evaluation found that Horsch had several characteristics associated with psychopathy, but he was not identified as psychopathic. Why?

One answer is that the tests used to identify psychopathic characteristics had not yet been developed in 1985. Although a precursor to the PCL-R was developed in 1980, it was not commercially available, and the PCL-R was not commercially released until 1991. Other psychopathy assessment tests were not developed until after the PCL-R.
Latest research on psychopathy
An astonishing level of research regarding psychopathy has been conducted since the early 1990s.

Some research has found that the introduction of psychopathy evidence in both American and Canadian courts has increased dramatically over the past few decades. In these cases, psychopathy evidence is primarily used by the prosecution to argue for a more severe punishment of a convicted defendant.

There is also evidence that psychopathy evidence is being inappropriately relied on in death penalty cases. The PCL-R has not been proven to predict violence among inmates on death row or in highly restrictive prison settings. However, it can reliably predict violence among inmates in less secure correctional settings and among individuals about to be released from incarceration.

Other research has focused on the brain structure and function associated with psychopathy. Studies have found that the brain region associated with thrill-seeking and impulsive behavior is larger among people with psychopathic characteristics, while regions associated with emotional regulation and fear processing are smaller.

Identifying psychopathic characteristics before someone engages in violence is the ideal. However, most psychological evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system take place only after the person has been arrested or convicted.

But if a psychological evaluation is conducted after an individual has been arrested for or convicted of a less serious crime, or when someone is showing early signs of antisocial behavior, the identification of psychopathic characteristics could help courts and treatment providers intervene before there is an escalation to violence.

articles.title: The ‘activity trap’: fear of losing benefits is stopping some disabled people from exercising
articles.author: Toni Williams, Associate Professor, Department of Sport and Exercise Sciences, Durham University
paras: For some people with disabilities, going swimming or attending an exercise class comes with a worry that many others would never consider: could being seen to be physically active lead to their disability benefits being stopped?

This fear is known as the activity trap. A new report published by Disability Rights UK draws on research I led at Durham University and developed with disabled people and disability organisations. Of the disabled people we surveyed, 80% worried that being physically active could put their benefits at risk.

Only one in five participants who had applied for or were receiving benefits were happy with how much physical activity they did. Nearly three-quarters said they would be more likely to increase their activity if they knew their benefits would not be affected.

Disabled people already face barriers to physical activity, including high costs and facilities that are difficult to access. Nearly 40% of disabled adults in England do less than 30 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week, according to Sport England. This means activity that makes someone breathe faster than usual, such as brisk walking. The proportion is almost twice that of non-disabled adults.
The activity trap was first highlighted in research published in 2018, when almost half of disabled respondents said they feared losing benefits if they were seen being active.
To explore how this fear affects people’s lives, we surveyed more than 200 disabled people and held group discussions with more than 30 participants. We also examined relevant laws and legal cases.

Participants described feeling encouraged to exercise to manage their health while worrying that being active could be taken as evidence that they no longer needed financial support. One participant said: “I would love to go to the gym, every day, but I don’t dare because I would be seen as being too physically fit.”
Others worried about being reported for benefit fraud if someone saw them enjoying an activity in public.

More than one-quarter of participants who had applied for or were receiving benefits reported having benefits or other financial support removed because of physical activity. These findings describe participants’ experiences; the survey alone cannot establish why individual benefit decisions were made.
How can physical activity affect benefits?

Much of our research focused on personal independence payment (PIP). This benefit helps with the extra costs of living with a disability or long-term health condition. People can receive it whether they work or not.

To decide who qualifies, officials assess how someone’s condition affects everyday activities, such as preparing food, washing and moving around. Going to the gym does not automatically mean someone will lose their benefits. But evidence of physical activity may be considered when deciding what someone can do.

Under existing PIP guidance, assessors must consider whether someone can carry out an activity safely, to a reasonable standard, as often as needed and without taking an unusually long time. They must also consider conditions that vary from day to day.

Yet participants told us that assessors sometimes appeared to place too much emphasis on isolated examples of physical activity, without adequately considering the pain, fatigue or other difficulties they experienced.

Our examination of legal cases revealed similar problems. In one 2024 upper tribunal case, a decision about a man’s entitlement to PIP had relied partly on observations of his ability to walk. However, the tribunal had failed to establish how far he could walk within a reasonable time, how frequently he needed to rest and whether he could repeat the activity. The upper tribunal ruled that the decision was legally flawed and ordered the case to be heard again.

The effects extended beyond physical activity. Of those who answered our survey question about the benefits application process, 84% said it had negatively affected their mental health. Some felt forced to concentrate on everything they could not do, while others said their own accounts or medical evidence were dismissed. The prospect of having to challenge a decision added to their anxiety.
These findings come as the UK government reviews PIP. The Timms review has acknowledged that the current system can discourage physical activity and participation in community life.

Our report calls for better training for assessors, independent advice for people applying for benefits or challenging decisions, and greater involvement of disabled people and organisations led by them in designing the assessment system. These changes could help ensure decisions reflect the realities of living with a disability, including conditions that fluctuate.

A benefits system intended to support the independence of people with disabilities must recognise that occasionally being physically active does not mean someone no longer needs financial support. The challenge now is to ensure that this principle is reflected in how benefits decisions are made.

articles.title: How Denmark became the sperm donation capital of the world
articles.author: Stine Willum Adrian, Professor in Sociology, University of Tromsø
paras: “They invaded us once by boat, and now they’re doing it with sperm!” Playful headlines like this are rapidly making Danish donor sperm as renowned as Danish bacon, Lego and designer furniture.

You may not (yet) be aware that Denmark is considered “the sperm capital of the world”. Apart from the US, it is the only country that not only fulfils its own demand for sperm through private sperm banks, but exports donor sperm to more than 100 countries.
This development feels surprising in a country like Denmark, where the welfare state provides universal, free healthcare and places a strong emphasis on reproductive care.

In other European countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, an estimated 60% of children born after sperm donation were conceived using Danish sperm. In Denmark itself, it’s estimated that around one in every 100 children is now born using donor sperm.

Health Gap / Sundhedskløften is a collaborative series from The Conversation UK and Denmark’s Videnskab.dk exploring what the two countries can learn from each other when it comes to health and wellbeing.

From cycling and alcohol to inequality, healthcare and everyday habits, the series looks beyond hospitals and medical treatment to explore how culture, politics and society shape the way people live – and how healthy they are.

So how did Denmark come to dominate the global sperm trade? Well, the introduction of cryotechnology in the 1950s changed things forever. Sperm could now be frozen, stored and transported, making donation safer, more flexible and, more importantly, scalable.

Freezing enabled screening for sexually transmitted infections after donation, reducing transmission risks. It also allowed sperm banks in Denmark to curate large catalogues of donors with diverse characteristics. This made international distribution possible, turning sperm into a transportable commodity.

By the 1970s, Denmark had established a public sperm bank supplying clinics across Denmark, Norway and Iceland. But when private fertility clinics emerged in the 1980s and 1990s alongside IVF, they fell outside this system.

That gap created an opening for Danish startup Cryos International, which now describes itself as the world’s largest sperm bank. Backed by private capital, the company expanded donor recruitment — particularly in university cities — and rapidly built a commercial catalogue.
It soon began supplying both public and private clinics as well as international customers, accelerating Denmark’s emergence as a global hub. Other private Danish sperm banks soon followed suit.

Danish sperm banks’ success has also depended on their ability to navigate different countries’ shifting regulations. Rules around anonymity, eligibility and export can change quickly between jurisdictions, forcing providers to adapt or lose access to markets.

Because the Danish sperm industry was already highly commercialised and geared towards international markets, companies were often able to adapt more quickly than sperm banks in other countries. For example, when the UK and Norway went from only allowing the use of anonymous donors to only allowing the use of non-anonymous donors in 2005, Danish sperm banks soon changed their practices to recruit both anonymous and non-anonymous donors.

At the same time, demand has changed. As male infertility treatments have improved, donor sperm use has increasingly been driven by single women and same-sex couples. Cryos International reports that around 60% of recipients are now single women, and 35% are in same-sex relationships — though access for these clients remains restricted in many countries.

Such restrictions used to apply in Denmark too. Until 2007, women without male partners could not access treatment through doctors there. Midwives, however, were not bound by the same rules. So, Danish midwife Nina Stork used this legal gap to establish an insemination clinic. It became a key destination for single women and same-sex couples across Europe.
When Danish law changed in 2007 to allow for same-sex couples – ahead of many other European countries – demand for treatment in Denmark increased further.

But the search for regulatory loopholes didn’t stop there. In 2011, Cryos began selling sperm directly for home insemination, classifying it under EU rules as a commodity rather than human tissue — effectively bypassing national restrictions in some countries.
This expansion was later curtailed after EU pressure led Denmark to tighten its rules requiring medical supervision for donor sperm use.

Donor sperm is not just a medical solution. It sits at the centre of ongoing ethical and political debates that, as my research into reproductive technologies in Denmark shows, tend to surface in similar ways across different countries.

Again and again, the same questions come up: who should have access to treatment? Who is considered suitable to donate? How much choice should parents have when selecting donors – and what kinds of relationships should be created between donors, families and donor-conceived children?

Part of what makes the field so contested is what this technology changes in practice. Donor conception separates sex from reproduction in a very direct way. It makes it possible for people — especially women — to have children without sexual intercourse, and to do so within systems that are increasingly structured, commercialised and cross-border.
In the future, sperm banks may need to address growing criticism about the amount of sperm a single man can donate, with some donors having fathered over 200 children globally.

Additionally, the widespread adoption of DNA testing among the general population, combined with advocacy from organisations representing donor-conceived individuals, has intensified the debate around donor anonymity.

It was recently revealed that a sperm donor in Denmark unknowingly carried a cancer-causing genetic mutation that was passed on through sperm used in fertility treatments across Europe between 2005 and around 2022. This resulted in nearly 200 children being conceived, some of whom have gone on to develop or die from cancer. This has prompted renewed calls for scrutiny of international sperm donation rules.

Indeed, two women have already sued the Danish state, arguing that access to information about one’s genetic origins is a fundamental human right. As a result, the practice of anonymous donation is facing mounting criticism.
Should Denmark decide to ban donor anonymity, the repercussions could extend well beyond the country’s borders – potentially reshaping sperm donation practices on a global scale.

articles.title: Is ​adding cottage cheese ​to everything from brownies to flatbreads really the best way to​ 'proteinmaxx’ – and do you even need to?
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: Cottage cheese used to be the sort of food you associated with 1970s diet plans, uninspiring lunches and people who claimed to enjoy eating grapefruit for breakfast.
Now it’s a TikTok sensation.

Social media creators are blending the curdy, clumpy white stuff into everything from cookie dough and chocolate brownies to flatbreads and even slapping it onto hot dogs. Apparently, there’s no recipe that can’t be improved with a generous helping of cottage cheese.
But why has this rather unglamorous dairy product suddenly become so fashionable?

The answer is protein. We’re in the middle of a protein boom, with supermarkets filling their shelves with high-protein yoghurts, cereals, puddings and snacks. Even tea, it seems, isn’t safe from the protein treatment.

Cottage cheese, naturally high in protein and relatively low in fat, has been embraced by fitness influencers who claim it can help build muscle and burn fat. But does the science support these claims?

That’s what my co-host, Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol, and I investigate in the first episode of the second season of Strange Health, The Conversation’s podcast exploring the weird and wonderful world of health and wellness trends.

To find out whether this unlikely superfood deserves its newfound celebrity status, I spoke to Dominic Farsi, a researcher at King’s College London, who’s become something of a resident cottage cheese expert for us.

We investigate what makes cottage cheese nutritious, whether it really helps with muscle growth and weight loss, and why the evidence behind some of its more extravagant health claims is less convincing than social media would have us believe.
Proteinmaxxing – how much is too much?

But cottage cheese is only part of a much bigger story. We also explore “proteinmaxxing”, the growing trend for deliberately consuming large quantities of protein through food, shakes, bars and supplements.

Protein is essential for maintaining muscle, repairing tissues and supporting the immune system. And some people, including older adults and those doing intensive resistance training, may benefit from consuming more.
But how much is enough? And can you have too much?
Dan explains why the benefits of increasing protein intake eventually level off, and what can happen when people take their protein obsession to extremes.

We even venture into the rather alarming history of “rabbit starvation”, a term used by early explorers to describe the potentially fatal consequences of surviving on exceptionally lean meat, such as wild rabbit, without enough fat or carbohydrates.

And we ask whether the source of your protein matters as much as the quantity, particularly when so many processed foods are being marketed as healthier simply because they’ve had extra protein added.
Have you spotted a bizarre health trend you’d like us to investigate? Email strangehealth@theconversation.com. The stranger the question, the better.

articles.title: Many vapes and e-cigarettes are now banned in Pennsylvania – here’s what Philly consumers and businesses need to know
articles.author: Ana Santos Rutschman, Professor of Law, Villanova University
paras: Many popular nicotine vapes are now banned in Pennsylvania, with only six companies approved to sell their products in the state after a legal ban went into effect on Oct. 19, 2026.
I am a health law professor at Villanova University outside Philadelphia.
Here’s how Pennsylvania’s new law works and what to expect as enforcement begins – especially in Philadelphia, where proximity to states with different laws might pose some challenges.
The products in question include e-cigarettes, vapes and other electronic nicotine delivery systems, commonly known as ENDS.
These products dispense an inhalable aerosol that contains nicotine and other chemicals, including flavoring agents.
ENDS are the most common form of tobacco used by teens and young adults. Flavored vapes are especially appealing to middle and high school students.

In recent years, a growing body of research has studied the health impact of ENDS use, particularly among younger smokers. These studies have raised concerns not only about long-term addiction to nicotine but also exposure to potentially carcinogenic or otherwise harmful chemicals. In 2018, the U.S. surgeon general declared youth vaping an epidemic.

At the federal level, ENDS are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration, but states have the authority to restrict their sale in order to protect the health of their citizens. This is precisely what Pennsylvania has done, joining more than a dozen other states with similar registry laws.
Some popular brands can still be sold

The new law requires the state attorney general to maintain a registry of ENDS approved for sale in Pennsylvania. If a product is not listed in the directory, businesses that sell them will face fines.

The directory currently includes products from just six manufacturers: Juul Labs, R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co., Blue Nine, Custom Technologies, NJoy and Schwartz E-Liquid. However, these manufacturers produce several of the most well-known brands of ENDS, and many of the products included in the directory are extremely popular, such as Juul vaporizers. The reason the new law allows these specific products to continue to be sold is that they have been evaluated by the FDA.

The directory does exclude some very popular products as well, including many brands of disposable vapes and vape juice. The law was designed to specifically ban products that have not been evaluated by the FDA.
If a business sells or offers to sell a product that is not in the directory, the consequences can be severe.

For first-time violations, there will be a fine of up to US$500 per product. A second violation within a year will trigger a fine of $1,000 per day per product until the product is either removed or appears listed in the directory. It will also lead to suspension of the license to sell tobacco products for at least 14 days. A third violation within a year will raise the fine to $1,500 per day per product, coupled with license revocation.

Attorney General David Sunday says his office will focus on “targeted enforcement.” What exactly targeted enforcement means is unclear, but the new law authorizes unannounced inspections. In addition to the premises, inspectors can also examine books and records.
Illegal products that are offered for sale will be subject to seizure and forfeiture, as well as destruction at the business’s expense.
The new law does not impose penalties on consumers who purchase banned products.
What to expect in Philadelphia

Philadelphia was an early adopter of a restrictive approach to the sale of vaping products due to concerns about the youth vaping epidemic. In 2019 the city banned the sale of certain flavored ENDS that were especially popular among adolescent and teen smokers.

Pennsylvania as a whole, however, has been less assertive than some of its neighbors, such as New York, in trying to stop youth vaping. The American Lung Association rates Pennsylvania in the D to F range for its tobacco control policies, below nearby New Jersey, New York and Delaware.

While the Pennsylvania law will reduce the number of products that can be legally sold in the state, it will still be relatively easy for a consumer in Philadelphia to travel to New Jersey or Delaware and buy some of the products banned under Pennsylvania law, including popular brands of disposable vapes.

But additional tobacco control measures may be underway, especially in Philadelphia. On Oct. 15 a member of the Philadelphia City Council introduced a bill that would amend zoning laws in a way that would effectively prevent new businesses selling tobacco and vaping products from opening in many areas of the city.

articles.title: The science and politics behind the panic over ultraprocessed foods
articles.author: Garrett M. Broad, Professor of Communication Studies, Rowan University
paras: Ultraprocessed foods have a terrible reputation.

Studies have linked them with multiple chronic diseases. Journalists and health influencers characterize them as poison. Some public health experts call for a global halt to producing and consuming them.

But the debate around ultraprocessed foods is not nearly as settled as it may seem. As a researcher who studies social movements for healthy and sustainable food, I have been documenting the history of processed foods and examining debates around the science and politics of ultraprocessing.
In basic terms, ultraprocessed foods are mass-produced, industrial formulations that use ingredients not typically found in a home kitchen, and that generally contain little to no intact whole foods.

Yet the very definition of ultraprocessed is highly contested. While a growing number of advocates say that ultraprocessing is dangerous to public health, skeptics counter that the fervor around the topic has become a moral panic, and insist that some ultraprocessed foods can be part of a healthy diet.
A brief history of food processing

People have been processing food – that is, transforming crops and animals into food ingredients and products – for all of human history. Cooking, which historians generally consider the first form of food processing, goes back as far as 2 million years. In the millennia and centuries that followed, people developed and refined other traditional food processing methods, including grinding, baking, fermenting, drying and pressing.

New types of food processing were created during the industrial age, beginning in the mid-18th century. Canning, pasteurization and refrigeration were among the major innovations that reshaped not only how people eat but society as a whole.

Before that time, nearly all food was local food – that is, produced within a few dozen miles – and people consumed fresh foods quickly to avoid spoilage. Food processing promised to improve food safety, shelf life, quality, convenience, taste and healthfulness. The world became more urbanized as regional and international supply chains developed. Geographically dispersed farmers were connected to retailers and consumers across the newly modern food system.

From the mid-20th into the 21st century, food manufacturers added a host of complex technological innovations to the food processing playbook. Their efforts made processed foods more standardized for the mass market and more convenient for consumers. But public health experts warned that processed junk foods were packed with salt, sugar and saturated fat – problematic nutrients linked to obesity, diabetes and other diet-related diseases.
Food processing and the NOVA framework

By the mid-2000s, some healthy food advocates began to argue that the nature and extent of food processing, rather than the presence of specific problematic nutrients, explained diet-related chronic disease. The journalist Michael Pollan famously implored his audience to avoid “edible food-like substances.” Instead, he advised: “Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.”

Brazilian epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro coined the term “ultraprocessing” in 2009 as part of his work on what he and colleagues called the NOVA classification. The NOVA framework establishes a four-category system that characterizes a food based on its level of processing.

NOVA Category 1 includes unprocessed or minimally processed plant or animal foods that are close to their natural state and contain no additives. Category 2 refers to processed culinary ingredients – that is, products derived from Category 1 via pressing, grinding or similar techniques. Category 3 describes processed foods made by combining Category 1 and Category 2 using traditional methods, such as baking, boiling or canning.

NOVA Category 4 foods are ultraprocessed foods, often described as industrially manufactured food products that can’t be made at home. Examples of ultraprocessing include separating whole foods into substances, chemically formulating foods or using cosmetic additives such as food dyes.

According to the framework, corporations design ultraprocessed foods to be convenient, hyperpalatable and highly profitable. They are packaged attractively, marketed intensively and intended to displace other food groups.

Today, ultraprocessed foods make up an increasingly large share of global diets. They account for more than 50% of total calories in the United States, with many low- and-middle income nations not far behind.
Since the NOVA framework emerged, researchers have tried to test whether food processing can explain how certain foods affect people’s health.

The vast majority of this work has explored correlations between consuming ultraprocessed foods and developing health problems. One consistent result stands out: People who consume more ultraprocessed foods are at higher risk for multiple chronic diseases and early death.

However, even that conclusion is more complex than it appears. It turns out that certain categories of ultraprocessed foods – such as sweetened beverages like sodas and processed meats like deli meats – are consistently associated with negative health outcomes including heart disease and stroke. But other ultraprocessed products – breads, cold cereals, yogurt and even savory snacks – have actually been correlated with lower rates of these health problems.
Still other ultraprocessed foods – including sauces, condiments and ready-to-heat dishes like frozen dinners – show no consistent links to people’s health one way or the other.

Only a handful of clinical trials that can actually show cause and effect have explored ultraprocessed foods’ effects on health. One prominent study did find that participants who ate a diet of ultraprocessed foods for two weeks consumed more calories and gained more weight than participants who followed a minimally processed diet, but other experiments have found no clear effect. What’s more, these studies generally last just a few weeks – far too short a time frame to draw conclusions about long-term health impacts.

Some food science researchers are unsurprised by these mixed findings, arguing that the definition of “ultraprocessed” is ambiguous and frequently subjective. For example, a cake prepared by a home baker would be considered a NOVA Category 3 “processed food.” But if that same cake were industrially manufactured using a commercial preservative, then packaged and sold at a grocery store, it would become a NOVA Category 4 “ultraprocessed food” – even if the two cakes were nutritionally identical.

Fundamentally, many nutrition scientists remain unconvinced that processing alone can explain why certain foods are associated with poor health. Instead, they emphasize that unhealthy ultraprocessed foods frequently have poor nutritional profiles and other qualities that make them easy to overeat. And they argue that making ultraprocessed foods healthier, not getting rid of them entirely, can improve public health.

Vilifying ultraprocessed foods may have harms, they suggest, like creating unnecessary fear and promoting disordered eating. It can also stigmatize eco-friendly, plant-based meats or ultraprocessed products such as baby formula that are designed for clinical nutrition.
The wholesale rejection of ultraprocessed foods could also make life more difficult for families who rely on the convenience and affordability the products offer.
Processing versus nutrients

On the other hand, many food policy and public health researchers maintain that the common definition of ultraprocessed is clear enough, especially if exceptions are made for healthy ultraprocessed foods. They also note that many supporters of ultraprocessed foods have ties to the food industry. They insist that the existing evidence is strong enough to take immediate policy action, including making changes to how ultraprocessed foods are produced, purchased and marketed.
Regulating ultraprocessed foods wouldn’t just benefit public health, advocates argue. It could also help rein in harms to food culture, business and the environment.

In this sense, ultraprocessed foods are a symptom of a bigger problem: an unsustainable industrial food system that is dominated by a handful of corporations. That argument, of course, is plenty contested too.

Ultimately, researchers and advocates from all sides of the debate mostly agree that the modern food environment needs to be made healthier. The key point of disagreement, however, is whether policymaking and dietary guidance should directly address ultraprocessing or stick to a more traditional focus on nutrients instead.

Garrett M. Broad is a board member with the non-profit Plant Based Foods Institute and an Advisory Board member with the non-profit New Jersey Food Democracy Collaborative, both on a non-remunerated basis. articles.title: What medical students learn from talking to care home residents
articles.author: Helen Rainford, Lead for Primary Care, School of Medicine and Dentistry, University of Lancashire
paras: I was very nervous at the start of the placement because I have always struggled with starting conversations. The idea of speaking with someone much older than me and focusing on non-medical topics felt quite daunting. I was worried I wouldn’t know what to say or how to keep the conversation going.
For this first-year medical student, visiting a care home was daunting. There was no medical history to take or diagnosis to make. The task was to get to know an older resident through conversation.

Listening and showing compassion are core expectations of medical graduates. Yet empathy can be difficult to develop and sustain. Some studies suggest it declines during medical training, particularly when students enter clinical settings, although other research reports mixed findings.

One possible explanation is the “hidden curriculum”: attitudes students absorb from doctors and clinical environments alongside formal teaching. A 2023 review of 16 studies identified heavy workloads and poor role models among influences that may encourage emotional detachment.
Doctors need to manage their emotions in distressing situations. How can medical schools also encourage students to remain curious about the people experiencing illness?
Getting to know the person
At the University of Lancashire, I developed The Person Before the Patient project, a care-home placement piloted in 2023/24. It was made compulsory for first-year medical students in 2024/25.

The programme operates across 11 care homes. During four-week placements, students meet residents who may be living with dementia, frailty or long-term conditions. Rather than assess medical needs, they learn about residents’ interests and experiences.

An Australian study of 61 fifth-year medical students found that five-day care-home placements improved dementia knowledge and attitudes towards working with older people, although some students questioned their educational value.

Our programme introduces students earlier, before their conversations become focused on clinical assessment. They may arrive with prepared questions, expecting predictable answers. Instead, they must respond to what residents choose to share.

I realised that I had to adapt my communication style. This meant listening more and allowing the resident to lead the conversation, rather than relying on prepared questions. I also learned to become comfortable with periods of silence while residents searched for the words they wanted to use.

The student also became more attentive to facial expressions and gestures. Such skills are useful when people experience hearing loss or memory difficulties. Nice guidance on dementia recommends adapting communication to people’s needs and considering their histories and preferences.
The placement gives students time to practise listening at a resident’s pace, something that can be harder during a busy clinical appointment.
Medical students often practise consultations with actors playing patients. These exercises develop communication skills, but can feel different from hearing someone describe their own life.

A New Zealand analysis of five students’ nursing-home reflections found that providing personal care sometimes helped students recognise residents as individuals. But encounters involving incontinence or frightening behaviour could leave students overwhelmed. In some accounts, they began describing residents as problems to manage rather than people to understand.

That small study examined hands-on caregiving, unlike our conversation-based placement. Nevertheless, it shows why students need support to reflect on difficult feelings instead of allowing discomfort to shape their attitudes towards patients.
One student on our placement wrote:
Being with the residents made me feel and understand what empathy actually is. Before this I feel I was ‘pretending’ to be empathetic with simulated patient in classes and exams.
The student went on to describe relating residents’ life experiences to their own family and feeling better able to empathise.

Of 281 students who undertook the placement, 157 voluntarily completed written reflections as part of a project with ethical approval. These accounts show what respondents felt they had learned. However, we did not formally measure empathy, and students who chose to respond may have felt more positively about the experience than those who did not.

A UK evaluation of the Time for Dementia programme found that students who regularly visited people with dementia and their families showed improvements in knowledge and attitudes, but no significant difference in measured empathy compared with other students. A review of long-term empathy training also found little evidence that gains persist.

For our programme, this means positive reflections are an encouraging starting point, but cannot establish lasting changes in empathy or clinical behaviour. A fuller evaluation would need to assess students over time, including after they begin clinical training, rather than relying on their immediate impressions.

Residents live in the homes where students learn, so they should be able to choose whether to take part and what they want to share. Otherwise, there is a risk of treating people’s lives as teaching material without giving them control over the encounter. Guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence emphasises residents’ involvement in choosing meaningful activities.
In some participating homes, residents took part in discussions about hosting students and, alongside staff, how placement funding would be used.
Care-home managers report that many residents enjoy the visits, look forward to students returning and become more socially engaged. These observations have not been independently evaluated.
An Australian study involving 28 residents found that healthcare student placements offered opportunities for social connection and enabled residents to contribute to students’ education.

Medical schools cannot remove the pressures future doctors will face. Spending time with older people without the demands of diagnosis or treatment may nevertheless help students see patients as people with lives beyond their medical needs.

articles.title: Cannabis is getting stronger, but doubling THC dose doesn’t get you twice as ‘high’ – new study
articles.author: Isabella Goodwin, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Neuroscience of Addiction, Australian Catholic University
paras: Cannabis products are getting more potent and easier to buy around the world. Yet little is known about how bigger doses of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main active ingredient in cannabis, change what people feel. Our new research found that larger doses generally make people feel more high, but not in a straight line. Doubling the dose does not double the feeling of intoxication.
This leaves a simple but important question for first-time and returning users: how will the amount of THC I take make me feel?

Cannabis laws have changed in many countries, and in some cases this has led to increased access to and diversity of products, as well as some increases in first-time cannabis users. Meanwhile, the amount of THC in cannabis products has been rising around the world, whether or not cannabis is legal.

THC is the part of cannabis that changes how you think and feel, and it produces both positive and negative effects. It does this by acting on receptors in the brain, mainly one called CB1. These receptors are part of the endocannabinoid system, which helps keep the body stable and protected.

First-time and inexperienced users are the most likely to take too much by accident and have unwanted effects, such as anxiety and paranoia. The huge range of products on the market makes it hard for them to judge how much is too much.

For our study, published in the journal Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, we combined evidence from 41 studies looking at the immediate effects of THC on how people feel. It included 1,020 participants who used cannabis less than once a week. In these experiments, people were given known doses of THC, and their reports were compared with those after a placebo (a dummy treatment), because simply believing you have taken THC can cause a mild high.
So how does THC change the way people feel? Overall, people who rarely used cannabis felt more high, anxious and tired, and less alert and content, than they did on the placebo.

We looked at the effects of inhaling a “Standard THC Unit” (5mg of THC), which is the proposed cannabis version of alcohol “units” or “standard drinks”. On a 100-point scale, after subtracting the effects of the placebo, a Standard THC Unit raised “high” by 34 points, “anxiety” by 14, “tired” by 26 and “calm” by five. It lowered “content” by 71 points and “alert” by 40.

Doubling the dose from 5mg to 10mg raised the intensity of the high only from 34 to 39 points – an increase of just 15%. This is common in pharmacology – the study of how drugs work – where bigger doses often bring smaller and smaller extra effects once a certain level is reached. (There was no change in anxiety, tiredness or alertness compared with the 5mg dose.)
For inexperienced users, this suggests that taking more THC can strengthen the effects they want, but the benefits may level off fairly quickly. Each extra dose adds less than the last.

Our results support the classic advice for reducing the risks of drug use: “start low, go slow”. Begin with a low dose and wait to feel the effects before taking more. The pleasurable effects may level off fairly quickly, but larger doses can still cause unpleasant experiences.
The cost of taking more THC

The brain adapts readily – when THC repeatedly activates the cannabinoid receptors, the brain temporarily reduces how many are available. You then need more THC to get the same high as before. This is known as tolerance, and it makes getting high more expensive.

The endocannabinoid system also helps the brain cope when it is under strain. It helps regulate sleep, appetite, pain, reward and, in particular, mood and stress. Research on this system suggests it is a bad idea to weaken it with heavy cannabis use. Long-term studies have found an increased risk of addiction and mental health problems in vulnerable people from frequent use of high-potency cannabis.

Our study has limits, though. Combining data from several studies is a strength of the meta-analysis approach, which pools the results of many studies, but the studies we included differed in many ways. They involved different participants, types of THC (some synthetic, some herbal), ways of taking it (vaping or joints), ways of measuring consumption and settings.

A next step is to test our findings directly in a controlled study where the same participants receive the most commonly used THC doses. Until then, our findings offer a simple message for people with little experience of cannabis: the high rises quickly at low doses, but extra THC soon adds less and less, which backs the advice to start low and go slow.

articles.title: Childhood adversity linked to billions in health and economic costs – new research
articles.author: Kat Ford, Research Fellow in the Public Health Collaborating Unit, Bangor University; Liverpool John Moores University
paras: Childhood trauma can leave scars that last long after the experiences themselves have ended. Its effects can reach into adult life, increasing the risk of mental illness, physical health problems and other difficulties.

Our latest research estimates that the health effects associated with adverse childhood experiences cost the equivalent of £7.8 billion in Wales and £115.6 billion in England in 2023. These figures represent 8.4% of Wales’s gross domestic product (GDP) and 5% of England’s.

These are not bills paid directly by governments. Instead, they put a monetary value on the burden of illness and premature death associated with childhood adversity, showing the scale of its potential effects on society.

Adverse childhood experiences are traumatic or highly stressful events. They include physical, verbal and sexual abuse, as well as experiences such as domestic violence, parental separation, or living with a family member who has mental health problems, misuses alcohol or drugs, or has been in prison.
Around half of adults in England and Wales report at least one such experience. About one in ten report four or more.

Research has consistently linked childhood adversity to poorer health and wellbeing in adulthood. People exposed to several types of adversity face greater risks of mental illness, chronic physical conditions and health-harming behaviour, like smoking and harmful alcohol use. Childhood adversity has also been linked to poorer education and employment outcomes and a greater likelihood of involvement in violence.
These consequences can increase demand for healthcare and other public services. Understanding the costs helps to show the scale of the problem and the potential benefits of investing in prevention.

We combined data from 10 studies conducted across England and Wales between 2012 and 2024. These studies interviewed adults about their childhood experiences and their health as adults. In total, we analysed data from 28,449 adults.

We examined seven causes of ill health, including mental illness, cancer, heart disease and stroke, alongside four health risks: smoking, high alcohol use, drug use and high body mass index. We explored links between childhood adversity and these outcomes, then used data from the global burden of disease study to estimate how much illness and premature death across the population could be associated with it.
Finally, we assigned a monetary value to these health effects using a government estimate of society’s willingness to pay to reduce ill health and premature death.

Drug use and violence showed some of the strongest links with childhood adversity. Our estimates suggest it was associated with around 60% of drug use in Wales and 57% in England. It was also associated with almost half of all violence: 49% in Wales and 46% in England.
However, the largest estimated financial costs came from mental illness and smoking. This is because these affect more people and account for a greater share of ill health overall.

In Wales, the estimated costs associated with childhood adversity were £1.8 billion for mental illness and £1.8 billion for smoking. In England, the figures were £37.8 billion and £22.7 billion respectively.
We also calculated regional estimates for England for the first time. These ranged from £6.3 billion in the north east to £18 billion in the south east.

Our findings strengthen the case for preventing childhood adversity and supporting children and families who experience it. Reducing exposure to trauma could help improve health across people’s lives, while potentially reducing the wider costs associated with illness and premature death.

There are several ways to help prevent childhood adversity. These include supporting parents, building life skills, challenging harmful social norms and addressing the social conditions that put families under pressure.

Awareness and action to address childhood adversity has increased across the UK. Evidence suggests that some adverse childhood experiences may be declining. But others such as verbal abuse and household mental illness have been less addressed and may even be increasing.

People affected by trauma also need effective support. Trauma-informed approaches, which recognise how past experiences can shape people’s needs and behaviour, are one way to improve that support. For example, the Trauma-informed Wales Framework sets out an approach to understanding and responding to trauma across society.

There are important limits to our findings. The estimates put a monetary value on health effects, including the value society places on reducing the risk of illness and premature death. They are not a direct measure of public spending or money that could automatically be saved through prevention. The study also identifies associations between childhood adversity and health outcomes, rather than proving that adversity caused every case.

Some vulnerable groups, including people in prison, were not represented in the surveys, despite being more likely to have experienced childhood adversity. Our estimates may therefore understate the true scale of the problem.

Even with these limitations, the findings highlight the potential scale of the health and economic burden associated with childhood adversity. Preventing trauma and providing better support for those affected could bring benefits that extend well beyond childhood.

articles.title: Treating depression during pregnancy may benefit baby’s brain development – new research
articles.author: Elysia Poggi Davis, Professor of Psychology, University of Denver
paras: Treating pregnant women’s depression with a short course of talk therapy doesn’t just improve their health – it can also shape how their babies’ brains develop before birth. That’s the finding of a new study we co-authored, published in the journal Nature Communications.

The study is part of an ongoing research project that explores how a form of brief interpersonal psychotherapy called MOMCare, which is specially tailored to treating prenatal depression, affects pregnant women with depression and their babies. MOMCare consists of eight 50-minute sessions focused on building interpersonal skills, reducing conflict and strengthening social support.

We enrolled 234 pregnant women who reported having symptoms of depression during their routine prenatal care appointments. Mothers joined the research project during the first or second trimester and were randomly assigned to one of two groups.

Women in one group received MOMCare. Women in the other group received education about mental health, strategies for managing depression symptoms and referrals to mental health support services, such as therapy, in the community. Both groups continued getting their usual medical care, which could also include referrals to therapy or medication.

In a previous publication, we found that 36% of moms enrolled in our study were diagnosed with depression in pregnancy before getting MOMCare and just 6% after it, showing the intervention was effective. Women who received the MOMCare intervention were also more likely to carry their baby to term, which is linked with shorter hospital stays after birth and improvements in many aspects of child health and development, including better school performance.

In the current study, to investigate how this form of talk therapy affects a baby’s developing brain, we measured the volume of different brain areas using an imaging technique called magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, within a few weeks of birth. We found that a brain area called the hippocampus, which plays a role in learning, memory and emotional regulation, was 5% smaller by volume in infants whose mothers received MOMCare compared to mothers in the other group.

Six months later, we brought the babies back into the lab to examine their emotional responses to unfamiliar experiences, such as encountering a noisy toy robot that danced and moved unpredictably. According to earlier studies, babies who respond more negatively to these tasks have higher levels of depression and anxiety in adolescence.
In our study, we found that babies with a smaller hippocampal volume at birth tended to respond less negatively than those with larger volume.

It may seem counterintuitive that a smaller brain volume is associated with stronger emotional regulation, particularly since in adults smaller brain volume is often associated with negative effects. However, in infancy the brain is growing, and faster growth may not always be advantageous. For example, one hypothesis proposes that stress can accelerate early brain development.

Depression affects up to 1 in 5 women during pregnancy. It also raises the risk of pregnancy complications such as high blood pressure and preterm birth. And having depression during pregnancy raises the risk of mental illness in the child.

Pregnancy offers a unique opportunity to simultaneously improve the health of both mother and baby. This is because women often have more contact with the healthcare system during pregnancy than at other times in their lives. Treating a woman’s depression during her pregnancy benefits two generations, improving the health of the mother and her developing baby.

Even though both MOMCare and the control condition in our study provided more support than pregnant women experiencing symptoms of depression often receive, we still saw a big difference between the groups. This suggests that a targeted intervention, even a noninvasive and relatively low-cost one such as MOMCare, can make a big difference.

Our study is the first to show that treating a woman’s depression during pregnancy may influence infant brain development. It aligns with a small but growing number of randomized clinical trials showing that reducing maternal depression has benefits for babies, including improved emotional development and changes in stress-related hormones.

These findings, if confirmed, could explain the biological underpinnings behind why treating prenatal depression is so critical. Further, they support public health initiatives to increase accessible mental health support during pregnancy.

It’s not clear how lessening mom’s depression in pregnancy leads to changes in the baby’s brain. It’s possible, for example, that stress-related hormones or inflammation associated with depression could influence brain growth.

Another open question is how the brain changes we observed might affect babies’ development long term. We hope to address this by continuing to follow mothers and babies through early childhood. By tracking conditions such as depression and anxiety as the children get older, we hope to determine whether treating mothers’ depression in pregnancy has lasting benefits for their children’s mental health and well-being.
The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

articles.title: Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death
articles.author: Jaquelyn Jahn, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology, Drexel University
paras: When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.
For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media have sounded the alarm about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons.

Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described as a sauna during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at SCI Muncy, told the Prison Journalism Project, “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.”

I am an epidemiologist who studies the health of incarcerated people. My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years.

While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s sixth-largest prison population among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons.

Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so extreme. Some, including the state correctional institutions in Cambridge Springs, Dallas, Laurel Highlands, Muncy, Waymart and Huntingdon, the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.

Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures pose risks to incarcerated people across the country, those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.
Prison healthcare systems under strain

Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease, and the state’s prison population is getting older, which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to 38 in 2023.
The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is US$3,357 per person per year. That’s 53% more than costs for younger incarcerated adults.

The state prison system experiences chronic staffing shortages of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time, because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.

Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs. But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers.

In Pennsylvania, they must pay a $5 copay per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from 23 cents to 50 cents per hour.
Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks

One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men.

This was unexpected because previous studies haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.

Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “accelerated aging” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease at a younger age than would typically be expected.
Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become life threatening during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable.
Preparing for a warmer climate

Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.

We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.
Jaquelyn Jahn receives funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Arnold Ventures, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

articles.title: Can social media bans protect young people’s mental health? Early research suggests that bans aren’t the answer
articles.author: Ari Lightman, Professor of Digital Media and Marketing, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: The year 2026 has been an expensive one for social media platforms.

Since March, YouTube and Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, have settled or paid out in multiple lawsuits to the tune of more than US$17 billion for allegedly acting negligently, deliberately designing their platforms to hook kids and misleading the public about safety and privacy. If these suits are any indication of how states and the public are starting to view social media platforms, more may follow.

On top of these lawsuits, social media platforms are facing a loss of business as bans for minors are accelerating and spreading worldwide. Australia was one of the first with a ban on kids under 16 on social media starting in December 2025, followed soon after by the U.K. with a similar prohibition.

The current list of countries looking to ban minors from these platforms tops more than 20, from Greece to the United Arab Emirates to Canada. The proposed and enacted bans around the world vary in terms of age restriction, parental consent rules and age verification methods. Different countries are looking at restricting different platforms, but most include a mix of Snapchat, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X.

These bans aren’t necessarily for mental health reasons only – some are motivated by political concerns about foreign-owned platforms, and others aim to protect young people’s privacy. But nearly every government banning social media platforms for young people mentions their mental health as a reason.

The question is, are these bans the solution to the mental health problems young people are facing? I research digital media and marketing and measure the impact of new technologies, and I’m skeptical about whether prohibiting access to these platforms will actually improve young people’s mental health.

Since Jonathan Haidt’s 2024 book “The Anxious Generation” critics of social media have increasingly focused on young people’s mental health. Haidt argues that social media disrupts kids’ social and neurological development, contributing to rising anxiety and depression through sleep loss, fragmented attention, addiction, loneliness, social comparison and perfectionism.
A 2026 study found that young people between 14 and 20 are more than 100% more likely to experience mental illness than 14- to 20-year-olds 50 years ago.

Increased use of social media and screen time is compounding an already precarious time for minors. In 2021 it was estimated that 20.5% of young people experienced elevated symptoms of anxiety, and 25.2% of youth reported elevated symptoms of depression globally.

Many factors contribute to this, including better screening and awareness of kids’ mental health problems, as well as societal disruptions as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. As the world sheltered in place and moved online for work, school and social interactions, there was an increase in isolation and loneliness.
In light of these concerns, some researchers argue that bans on social media platforms are like putting an age restriction on buying alcohol or cigarettes.

But unlike these addictive and potentially harmful substances, there are benefits to social media, especially for teens who feel disconnected from their local communities and want to build relationships with others who feel similarly.
Social media platforms allow for global connectivity and community-building with like-minded groups. They also provide a place for self-expression and civic engagement.
In a Pew survey of U.S. teens, 80% said social media helps them stay connected to what’s happening in their friends’ lives.
One place where the comparison with tobacco is actually quite apt is in relation to the money from lawsuit settlements.

In 1998, states settled a lawsuit against the major tobacco companies to recover smoking-related healthcare costs. Part of the settlement was allocated to programs aimed at reducing youth smoking. In 2026, total state funding for these programs amounts to just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion in revenue states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.

Similarly, some money from an August 2026 Meta settlement with a group of states for $17 billion is slated for state-based programs focusing on mental health infrastructure, school and community programs, and public health campaigns.
However, there is no oversight or direction as to how states should use the funds, nor is there a mechanism to report how that money has improved kids’ mental health care, safety and well-being.

Early evidence from the Australian social media ban shows that kids are finding work-arounds: Roughly 61% of kids ages 12–15 continue to access platforms using false IDs, altered appearances or virtual private networks, or VPNs, even though millions of accounts were disabled. In fact, this has become so common that U.K. lawmakers are debating restricting consumer VPN access.

Some countries, such as Australia, require the platforms themselves to develop ways of verifying a user’s age. Some minors have bypassed scans from biometric age estimation technology by using photo manipulation software, substituting celebrity photos, using clever makeup and even utilizing older friends and parents to pass the “selfie tests” on their behalf. Others simply manipulate their birth years during registration or rely on existing adult-verified accounts managed by family members.
And all of these age-verification methods, whether developed by a government or a social media platform, rely on collecting sensitive data to estimate age accurately, which creates privacy concerns.

Australia is currently seeking to raise fines on social media platforms that fail to comply with its requirements. The Australian safety commissioner, charged with enforcing the ban, issued a compliance update that showed 7 in 10 children who held accounts in restricted platforms remained on those platforms, and more than 80% of Australian teens ages 10-15 still use social media frequently.
Beyond concerns about enacting and enforcing these restrictions, some policymakers also worry that total bans could push some kids to migrate to even riskier online spaces.
Based on the evidence, I’m not convinced that banning social media platforms will be an effective solution to the mental health crisis among young people today.
Supporting young people’s mental health is a complex endeavor that will require a combination of people, organizations and resources coming together.

I believe kids’ mental health would be better served by governments enforcing safety by default standards on social media platforms rather than outright bans. This means that the highest security and privacy options are in place by default so that minors still on a platform are protected. For instance, accounts would be unsearchable by default, so users would have to intentionally make a profile change to be found by people they don’t know in real life.

Safety by default standards also place limits on the manipulation, algorithmic restraint and other addictive mechanisms that may lead to psychological harm in vulnerable populations such as young people.
Educating kids on digital literacy and online safety as well as ensuring some screen-free time are also going to help support kids’ mental health.

It’s also important for parents and other caregivers to recognize changes in behavior as a result of addiction to social platforms and screens. And when adults start seeing signs of a problem, they need clear, easy and affordable ways to connect their kids to mental health support, which is not available in most places right now.

And finally, the United Nations recommends bringing kids into the conversation about what’s best for them online. Obviously, this does not mean putting 12-year-olds in charge of regulatory agencies. But feedback from young people about what they care about, what they get out of being online and what makes it hard for them to look away from their screens could inform changes to social media platforms and education programs that could help young people engage online more safely and maintain a healthy balance.
Ari Lightman is affiliated with Jewish Healthcare Foundation

articles.title: Can AI screen for heart disease using photos of your tongue and face?
articles.author: David C. Gaze, Senior Lecturer in Chemical Pathology, University of Westminster
paras: An AI system trained on photographs of the face and tongue correctly identified every patient with coronary heart disease (CHD) in a small test, according to a new study from China.

The researchers recruited 518 people: 200 with diagnosed CHD and 318 healthy volunteers. Each had their face and tongue photographed with a purpose-built scanning system. The pictures were analysed using deep learning, a type of AI that learns to spot patterns in images.

The system examined the tongue and face photographs separately, then combined what each had picked up to predict who had CHD. Using both together performed better than either alone. The best-performing version was 98% accurate in a test of 104 people, correctly identifying all 40 patients with CHD, although two healthy participants were wrongly classified as having the condition – so-called “false positives”.

The AI focused on the centre of the tongue, its surface coating, the skin around the mouth and the cheeks. Some patients with CHD had darker tongues, thicker coatings or changes in facial pigmentation. The researchers say the areas highlighted by the AI are consistent with traditional Chinese medicine teachings about links between the tongue, face and heart.

Reading disease from appearance is not unique to traditional Chinese medicine. Doctors have long recognised that some visible features can point to underlying medical problems. Blue lips can signal low oxygen levels in the blood, and fatty yellow deposits around the eyelids, known as xanthelasma, can point to very high cholesterol, often caused by an inherited condition.

Whether a tongue or a cheek can reveal blocked arteries is a different matter. Skin tone, lighting, age, medication and smoking all change how a face and tongue look, and the study does not establish that these features are caused by blocked coronary arteries. AI may pick up associations that humans struggle to recognise, but that does not explain what causes them.

CHD develops when the arteries supplying the heart muscle narrow because of fatty deposits called plaques, a process known as atherosclerosis. This restricts blood flow and can eventually cause a heart attack. For many people, the first sign of a problem is chest pain, a heart attack or another life-threatening event, so spotting the disease earlier is an important goal of preventive medicine.

Doctors currently estimate risk using factors including age, smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes. If CHD is suspected, tests can include an electrocardiogram (ECG), blood tests or specialised scans. A quick, painless, low-cost photographic test could help decide who needs those investigations, particularly in communities where access to specialist healthcare is limited.
A promising result, with questions remaining

The study, published in Scientific Reports, compared people already diagnosed with CHD against healthy volunteers, which is very different from screening the general public, where people have a mix of other illnesses and levels of cardiovascular risk. The photographs were also taken under controlled lighting with specialised equipment.

The model has not been tested on people from other hospitals or settings. AI systems sometimes perform very well on the data used to build them but less well in different hospitals, ethnic groups or healthcare settings.

Not all the healthy volunteers were assessed with coronary imaging, so undetected disease cannot be ruled out. The AI may also have been picking up differences linked to age, other illnesses or other characteristics of the participants rather than heart disease.
Screening adds a further problem. Even a highly accurate test can produce large numbers of false-positive diagnoses when it is used on a population in which the disease is relatively uncommon.

Larger studies following people over time would need to show whether this approach can pick up disease that has gone unnoticed, tell it apart from other conditions and lead to better health. Researchers would also need to compare it directly with existing ways of assessing risk. If it proves useful, it could eventually be used alongside standard heart disease risk checks, cholesterol tests and blood pressure measurements.
