articles.title: Vaccines have been so successful that some people have forgotten why we need them
articles.author: Dan Stratton, Lecturer Biomedical Health Science, The Open University
paras: Three measles-related deaths have been reported in England in 2026. One child died from an acute infection, another from the long-term effects of measles, and an adult with an underlying immune condition also died.

Yet misconceptions about vaccination persist, including the belief that improved hygiene and sanitation have made vaccines unnecessary. Why do such claims continue to attract support when the evidence for vaccination is so strong?

Vaccination’s success partly explains this. In highly vaccinated countries, diseases that once killed or disabled millions have become so uncommon that many people have never witnessed their consequences. As the threat of disease becomes less visible, the perceived risk of vaccination can begin to outweigh the perceived risk of infection.

Vaccine scepticism also reflects concerns about personal freedom and distrust of pharmaceutical companies or governments. Research identifies confidence in vaccines, perceived disease risk and access as important influences on vaccination decisions.
Social media can amplify misleading claims. A 2024 review linked seeking information on social media with less favourable attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccines, although findings varied.
What happens when vaccination rates fall?
In January 2026, the World Health Organization confirmed that the UK had lost its measles elimination status. This followed evidence of sustained transmission in 2024.

England recorded 2,911 laboratory-confirmed measles cases in 2024, the highest annual total since 2012. Cases fell to 958 in 2025, but had already reached 1,030 by 12 October 2026, with children aged ten and under accounting for 61%.
In 2025-26, only 83.8% of children in England had received both doses of the MMR vaccine by their fifth birthday, well below the 95% target needed to help prevent outbreaks.
By 8 October 2026, the US had recorded 4,080 confirmed measles cases, exceeding the total for the whole of 2025.

Although most people recover from measles, it can cause pneumonia, inflammation of the brain (encephalitis), hearing loss and death. Rubella during pregnancy can cause miscarriage or serious congenital abnormalities. Polio can cause paralysis, while whooping cough can be fatal for young infants.
Did sanitation improvements defeat infectious diseases?

Vaccine critics sometimes argue that infectious diseases were already declining before vaccination, thanks to improved sanitation and nutrition. There is some truth to this historical observation. Better sanitation reduced the spread of waterborne infections such as cholera and typhoid, while better nutrition and healthcare helped people survive infections. But these improvements cannot explain the dramatic fall in measles following vaccination.

Before measles vaccination was introduced in 1968, England and Wales recorded between 160,000 and 800,000 measles notifications annually, with around 100 deaths each year. Cases subsequently fell dramatically as vaccination coverage increased.
Smallpox was eradicated through global vaccination and surveillance programmes. Worldwide cases of polio caused by wild poliovirus have fallen by more than 99% since 1988.
A 2024 study estimated that vaccination programmes prevented 154 million deaths worldwide between 1974 and 2024, most of them among children under five.
How do vaccines protect people?

Vaccines prepare the immune system to recognise an infectious organism before someone encounters it. Different vaccines achieve this in different ways. Some contain weakened or inactivated pathogens, while others contain harmless components of them. Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines provide instructions that allow the body’s cells to produce a particular antigen, a substance recognised by the immune system.

These approaches stimulate immune responses, including the production of antibodies and the development of memory B and T cells. If someone later encounters the pathogen, the immune system can respond more rapidly and effectively.
Vaccines cannot always prevent infection, but they can substantially reduce the risk of serious disease.

Critics sometimes claim that combined childhood vaccines, such as the measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox (MMRV) vaccine or the six-in-one vaccine, overwhelm a child’s immune system. Scientific evidence does not support this concern.

Addressing concerns that multiple vaccines could cause autism, a US study comparing 256 children with autism and 752 without autism found no link between the condition and exposure to vaccine components that stimulate the immune system.
A separate Danish study involving 657,461 children found no increased risk of autism following MMR vaccination.

People should be able to make informed decisions about medical treatment. However, infectious diseases introduce a complication: one person’s vaccination decision can affect other people’s health. High vaccination coverage helps limit the circulation of infectious diseases through what is known as herd immunity. That protection depends on maintaining high uptake across communities, rather than relying on national averages.
This helps protect people who cannot receive certain vaccines or may respond poorly to them, including young infants and people with suppressed immune systems.
For measles, at least 95% coverage with two doses of a measles-containing vaccine is needed in each community to help prevent outbreaks.
Why trust remains important

Concerns about pharmaceutical companies cannot simply be dismissed. The industry has a history of genuine misconduct, including GlaxoSmithKline’s 2012 guilty plea involving unlawful marketing and failure to report safety information about certain prescription medicines. Such cases demonstrate why independent regulation and transparent safety monitoring are necessary. They also help explain why some people are wary of reassurances from the industry itself.

Vaccines, like other medicines, can cause side effects. Most are mild, such as soreness at the injection site or a temporary fever. Serious allergic reactions are extremely rare. One large US study, for example, estimated approximately 1.3 cases of anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, per million vaccine doses.
Ongoing studies and monitoring programmes investigate suspected adverse reactions.
Public health communication also needs to acknowledge uncertainty and take people’s questions seriously. Dismissing concerns without explanation can reinforce existing distrust.
Restoring confidence requires clear information about what vaccines can and cannot do, alongside accessible vaccination services and honest discussion of potential risks.
The return of measles demonstrates what happens when protection against infectious diseases weakens.
Vaccination substantially reduces the risk of serious illness while helping protect people who are especially vulnerable. Its success should not cause societies to forget why it became necessary.

articles.title: Restraint can leave mental health patients traumatised. New research reveals what they need afterwards
articles.author: Nutmeg Hallett, Associate Professor of Mental Health Nursing, University of Birmingham
paras: Most of us know what it feels like to be ill and frightened. Now imagine being held down by the very people responsible for your care.

This can happen in mental health hospitals when staff believe someone poses a risk to themselves or others. Patients may be physically restrained, locked in a room alone or given medication to calm them quickly. These measures are known as restrictive interventions. Although they are intended to prevent harm, they can cause serious injuries and, in extreme cases, death.

Our research suggests that what happens after a restrictive intervention can affect how people recover from the experience. The support they receive may help them feel safe again, while a lack of support can add to their distress.

Concerns about the use of force in mental health care go back almost 200 years. In 1839, psychiatrist John Conolly introduced a policy at Hanwell Asylum in Middlesex that ended the use of mechanical restraints such as straitjackets and handcuffs. However, historical research shows that Conolly continued to advocate locking patients in rooms alone, a practice known as seclusion.

Today, restrictive interventions remain part of mental health care. Research has shown that these experiences can be deeply distressing and sometimes traumatic, even when staff consider them necessary to prevent harm.

Some patients experience nightmares, intrusive memories or symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) long after the intervention has ended. A review of patients’ experiences of mental health hospitals also found that fear of restraint could discourage people from seeking help.
Yet much less attention has been paid to what hospitals can do to support people afterwards.

A 2022 review of 21 studies found that patients frequently reported feeling frightened, powerless and unheard during restrictive interventions. Many also described poor communication from staff afterwards, leaving them with unanswered questions about what had happened. Some felt that once the immediate incident was over, it was forgotten by the staff involved. For the patient, however, the experience could remain distressing for months or even years.
We wanted to understand how mental health services could respond more effectively.

In our research, we examined 35 research publications and policies obtained from 46 NHS mental health trusts in England. We also worked with patients, carers and mental health staff to understand what people need following restrictive interventions.

Although NHS guidance recommends that patients receive support and have opportunities to discuss incidents, a separate analysis of hospital policies found considerable variation in how that support was described and organised.
Support needs to continue beyond the incident
One important finding was that talking about what happened can be valuable, but the timing and approach are crucial.

Immediately after being restrained, someone may still be frightened, angry or overwhelmed. They may need reassurance, practical help or simply some time and space before they feel ready to discuss the experience.
Being offered a conversation at that moment may feel like another demand rather than an opportunity for support.
But if a patient declines to talk immediately, they may receive no further opportunity. Our research suggests that declining a conversation should not mean losing access to support altogether.
Instead, support should continue, with opportunities to discuss what happened when the person feels ready.

When patients do want to talk, their needs may differ. Some want to describe how the experience affected them, while others want to understand why staff acted as they did. They may also want to explain what could have been handled differently.

Whatever the conversation involves, patients want to feel listened to, understood and taken seriously. Having some choice over when and where the conversation happens, and who takes part, can help restore a sense of control after an experience in which they may have felt powerless.

Our research also found that people wanted to know their concerns had made a difference. This could mean changes to their individual care plan or improvements in how the hospital responds to similar situations.
Without any visible response, conversations risk becoming a box-ticking exercise that leaves patients feeling dismissed.
Providing this kind of support also depends on the wider hospital environment. Staff need the time and support to listen to patients, reflect on what happened and act on what they learn.

A frightening experience cannot be undone. But being ignored or dismissed afterwards can deepen the harm, while compassionate support may help patients begin to rebuild their trust in the people caring for them.

The findings offer a lesson that extends beyond mental health hospitals. When someone has experienced something frightening, the way others respond afterwards can become an important part of their recovery.

articles.title: Cardiac arrest: why the quality of CPR could affect your chances of survival
articles.author: Melinda McPherson, Phd Candidate, Paramedic Science, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: When someone has a cardiac arrest, the actions of people nearby can make the difference between life and death. For years, the message has been clear: start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) as quickly as possible, even if you’ve never been trained.
That advice remains essential. But growing evidence suggests that how CPR is performed could also influence someone’s chances of survival.

Cardiac arrest happens when the heart suddenly stops pumping blood around the body, depriving the brain and other vital organs of oxygen. CPR involves pressing repeatedly on the chest to keep some blood circulating until emergency help arrives.

Starting CPR promptly can double or even triple someone’s chances of survival. Yet survival remains low. In England in 2024, only 9.5% of people survived for 30 days following an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in which ambulance crews attempted resuscitation.

Survival depends on several factors, including how quickly CPR begins, whether the cardiac arrest is witnessed and whether a defibrillator is available. But researchers are increasingly interested in another question: how effectively are members of the public performing CPR before paramedics arrive?

A 2026 Australian study examined 17,715 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in New South Wales between 2021 and 2024. Researchers found that patients who received CPR judged by paramedics to be good quality had substantially higher odds of surviving for 30 days than those who received no CPR.

CPR judged to be of a poor quality was not associated with a statistically significant improvement in survival compared with no CPR. This does not mean that poor-quality CPR is ineffective: the study could not establish whether it offered a benefit.

However, these findings need careful interpretation. The study was observational, so it cannot establish that differences in perceived CPR quality directly caused the differences in survival. Paramedics’ assessments were also subjective, and CPR quality was not recorded for every case.
Nevertheless, the findings reinforce the importance of giving members of the public the knowledge and support needed to perform effective chest compressions.

When the heart stops pumping, blood flow to the brain rapidly falls. Chest compressions help maintain circulation until paramedics can provide more advanced treatment. A public-access defibrillator can also assess the heart’s rhythm and deliver an electrical shock if one is needed.
The UK’s Resuscitation Council guidelines recommend pressing firmly in the centre of an adult’s chest at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions a minute, to a depth of around 5 to 6cm.

Compressions should be interrupted as little as possible, and the chest should be allowed to return to its normal position between each push. These recommendations are designed to help maintain blood flow while avoiding unnecessary interruptions.
The difficulty of measuring CPR quality
In England, national cardiac arrest reports record whether CPR was provided by a member of the public, but published figures do not routinely show how effectively chest compressions were performed.

Paramedics arriving at the scene may be able to judge whether compressions are being delivered effectively. However, these observations are not always recorded consistently, making it difficult to compare cases or identify where improvements are needed.

The Australian research offers one approach. Paramedics assessed bystander CPR as either good or poor quality, allowing researchers to examine its association with survival. But without a standardised, objective method of assessment, such judgments have limitations.
More consistent recording could help ambulance services understand which aspects of CPR people find difficult and where additional training or guidance might help.

For example, people may understand that they need to press on someone’s chest but be uncertain about how hard or how quickly to push. Better information about what happens during real emergencies could help shape training and improve the instructions given by emergency call handlers.

And support is already developing. In the east of England, ambulance services have introduced a pilot using live video to help specialist paramedics guide people through CPR while waiting for an ambulance.
This gives emergency staff an opportunity to see what is happening and offer more specific advice about chest compressions.
Encouraging people to act remains essential
The number of people receiving CPR from members of the public has increased in some countries. In England, bystanders provided CPR in 73% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest cases in 2024.

In Victoria, Australia, 80% of bystander-witnessed cases in which ambulance crews attempted resuscitation received bystander CPR in 2024-25, although the two figures cover different groups of patients.
There is still considerable room for improvement. Across Europe, the average reported bystander CPR rate is 58%, with substantial differences between countries.
Encouraging more people to intervene remains a public health priority. But in areas where bystander CPR is already common, improving its quality could offer another opportunity to increase survival.
This should never become a reason for someone to hesitate. A person witnessing a cardiac arrest cannot be expected to perform CPR perfectly, particularly in a frightening and unfamiliar situation.

Anyone who finds someone unresponsive should call 999 immediately. If the person is not breathing normally, the caller should begin CPR and follow the emergency call handler’s instructions. If a defibrillator is available, someone else can retrieve it while chest compressions continue.

The priority must always be to get people to act quickly, rather than worry about getting every compression right. But understanding what happens when bystanders perform CPR in real emergencies could help ambulance services give better guidance and support.
The aim is to make effective CPR easier for more people to deliver, and give those suffering a cardiac arrest a better chance of survival.

articles.title: Ketamine’s role in alleged Cornell rape highlights flood of psychoactive drugs on campus
articles.author: Christopher P. Holstege, Professor of Emergency Medicine and Pediatrics, University of Virginia
paras: Former Cornell student Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026 alleging that seven fraternity members raped her at a party, said the young men who assaulted her pressured her into taking the drug ketamine.

As an emergency room physician, medical toxicologist and the head of student health services at the University of Virginia, I have had a front-row seat to the growing danger that psychoactive substances such as ketamine present to the health and safety of university students.

Ketamine and its emerging spin-off versions are part of a wave of new and evolving designer drugs entering the United States and other countries. How widely these substances are used remains unknown, since most hospitals are unable to detect them on standard urine drug screens. But ketamine and other drugs are being increasingly reported as agents used in sexual assault – either when people take these drugs voluntarily, are pressured to take them or are given them covertly.
The increasing prevalence of ketamine and other drugs – and their use in sexual assault – is playing out on college campuses across the U.S. and putting students at risk.

Ketamine is a synthetic chemical that was first synthesized in 1962. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it as a general anesthetic for people and animals in 1970, and doctors and veterinarians used it for decades to induce anesthesia during surgeries and to relieve pain.

People have used ketamine recreationally since the 1970s. Getting high on it became more popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, when it was called “Special K.” It was frequently found in the club drug scenes and was associated with raves into the 1990s. Today, ketamine is sold on the street under a variety of slang names, such as K, Ket, and Vitamin K.

In 2019, the FDA approved a nasal spray version of ketamine, called esketamine, to treat depression that does not respond to other treatments. That drug’s use is tightly regulated, but clinicians are increasingly prescribing ketamine “off-label” for a variety of psychiatric conditions, including post-traumatic stress disorder.

Cases of poisoning caused by ketamine in the U.S. doubled between 2019 and 2023, according to an analysis of calls to poison control centers nationwide, and are now the highest they’ve ever been. This surge is in part due to the more widespread medical use of ketamine, which makes accessing it much easier. But street versions of the drug are also prevalent as chemists in basement laboratories create novel ketamine analogs.
Ketamine’s effects on the body

Ketamine’s effects vary depending on the dose and the person. It can cause someone to dissociate, creating an altered state of consciousness, changing what’s perceived through the senses and causing a sense of detachment from one’s self and one’s surroundings. The drug can also cause coma at high doses.

Someone who orally consumes ketamine would typically begin to feel its effects within 20 minutes. If they inhale or inject it, the effects are almost immediate. The primary effects generally wear off in less than an hour, but a person’s senses may remain dulled and their judgment and coordination impaired for several hours afterward.

Ketamine can cause a slew of other side effects, including delirium, amnesia, increased salivation, abnormal eye movements, high blood pressure and potentially fatal breathing problems. Alcohol and other drugs can interact with ketamine to worsen these effects significantly.

Ketamine is generally sold illegally as either a colorless, odorless liquid or a white or off-white powder. Either form can be easily and covertly placed into an unsuspecting person’s beverage or food. Ketamine can be snorted, and it can be smoked or vaped on products such as marijuana.
Ketamine and other drugs in sexual assault

Research is extremely spotty on how often a perpetrator of rape or sexual assault uses a chemical agent – whether ketamine, alcohol or another substance – to alter a victim’s senses. Research suggests that most often both parties use mind-altering substances voluntarily, although the effects of these substances can alter a person’s ability to grant consent.

Even so, there are numerous reports of perpetrators spiking a victim’s drink or otherwise slipping a drug to them without their knowledge. According to one study, 4.2% of rape victims were drugged covertly, though how often this actually happens is undoubtedly underreported.

That’s because it’s very hard to detect drugs taken this way. Most of the substances used to facilitate sexual assaults are rapidly absorbed and metabolized by the body, rendering them difficult to detect in routine urine and blood drug screenings. Another issue is that many days may have elapsed between the victim ingesting the drugs and their subsequent treatment at a medical facility.

Victims of rape or sexual assault are often reluctant to report incidents because of a sense of embarrassment, guilt or perceived responsibility, or because they may know their attacker. Some may not trust that their institution or local law enforcement will support them.

In my experience, the involvement of ketamine or other drugs invariably makes a bad situation worse – complicating consent, impairing judgment and reducing inhibitions. Ketamine causes confusion and drowsiness, and its sedative, hypnotic and memory-erasing properties can diminish a survivor’s recollection of events surrounding the sexual assault.

The availability of these drugs in the U.S., including on college campuses, has risen sharply – particularly since the early 2010s, as a slew of new substances have emerged and international drug control efforts have not kept up. Without more active education and prevention efforts, as well as better detection methods for these drugs, students will continue to pay the price.

articles.title: Cannabis doesn’t make you violent – despite what recent reports have claimed
articles.author: Simon C Moore, Professor of Public Health Research, Co-Director of Crime and Security Research Institute and Director of the Violence Research Group, Cardiff University
paras: In what looked like a return to the dark days of Reefer Madness – a 1936 film that portrayed cannabis as a drug that could drive people to madness and murder – a recent article in the Daily Telegraph claimed that cannabis users are “twice as likely to be violent”.

The claim comes from a systematic review by King’s College London that combined 63 studies covering more than 265,000 people. The researchers did, indeed, find a link between cannabis use and violence, but the headline overstates what the numbers can tell us.
There are three reasons to be cautious: other factors that could explain the link (known as confounders), the way the studies were designed, and potential biases in how the data was gathered.

Poverty, alcohol, other drugs and a difficult upbringing are all linked to violence in their own right. Cannabis is also illegal in many places, and buying it can bring people into contact with people and places where violence is more common. Some of these factors are more common among cannabis users, so these confounders could partly explain the link.

Ice cream sales rise and fall alongside drownings, yet nobody thinks ice cream causes drowning. Hot weather makes people eat more ice cream and swim more, linking the two. Cannabis and violence may be connected in a similarly roundabout way.

The review did try to account for other factors. But its authors generally favoured the versions of studies that adjusted for the fewest of these factors, making it harder to rule out alternative explanations.

Of the 63 studies in the review, 46 were cross-sectional, meaning they measured cannabis use and violence at one point in time. This makes it difficult to tell whether cannabis use came before the violence, followed it, or simply occurred alongside other circumstances that contributed to it. These studies found the strongest link between cannabis use and violence.

Studies that follow people over time – called longitudinal studies – can help establish which came first. These studies found a much weaker link between cannabis use and violence than the cross-sectional studies.

In the one-off studies, the odds of violence were more than twice as high among cannabis users. The Telegraph presented these figures as meaning cannabis users were up to twice as likely to be violent. In the longitudinal studies, cannabis users had 17% higher odds of violence than non-users.

It should also be noted that twice the odds is not the same as twice as likely. Likelihood looks at your chance out of the entire group. Odds compares the people an event happens to against those it doesn’t.
The two are close when violence is rare, but they drift apart when it is common.
For example, if one in 100 people experience something, doubling the likelihood gives you two in 100 (2%). Doubling the odds gives you two in 101 (1.98%) – a tiny distinction.

The gap widens a lot when an event is common. Imagine something that already happens to 50 out of 100 people. Twice as likely doubles that 50% chance to 100% (it happens to everyone). Twice the odds only increases that 50% chance to 67%.

One of the review’s authors told the Telegraph that a study of this size lets researchers “speak with more confidence about the risks”. That is true only in a narrow sense. Imagine measuring a room with a slightly stretched tape measure: a thousand repeat measurements might give a consistent answer, but the wrong one.

A large sample reduces random error – the chance that researchers happen to study an unusual group of people. It cannot fix systematic bias, where the original studies measured the wrong things or measured them badly.

Bias can creep in at every stage. Studies disagree on what counts as cannabis use (once, in the past month or daily?) and violence (a shove, a fight or a criminal conviction?). The review groups together domestic incidents, sexual assault, fights and robbery, which may have very different causes.

Results across the 63 studies also varied widely. Three analyses of the same US national drug survey, all included in the review, produced odds ratios ranging from about 1.3 to nearly 10. This may reflect differences in how cannabis use and violence were defined and measured, as well as in who was surveyed.

Also, some studies may be missing because research showing little or no link is less likely to be published. This could make the link between cannabis and violence look stronger than it is. The review found signs of this problem, and its attempts to account for it could not rule it out.

Finally, the review’s supplementary material rates the certainty of the evidence as very low. In other words, the authors have very little confidence in the size of their estimate, though they consider the association itself likely to be real. This important qualification does not appear in the Telegraph report.

None of this means cannabis and violence are unrelated, and the authors themselves acknowledge many of these limitations. But the headline figure leaves readers with a number that looks much more certain than the evidence warrants.

articles.title: Why adoptive families can struggle to get help until they reach crisis point
articles.author: Claire Agius, Lecturer/Researcher, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: In a deeply personal passage of his first Labour Party conference speech as UK prime minister, Andy Burnham paid tribute to the care workers who had looked after his father, Roy, who had Alzheimer’s disease and had died just two weeks earlier.

Those workers were “holding a threadbare system somehow together”, he said, yet remained “invisible to the political class of this country”. Addressing them directly, he added: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you.”

His words made me think about the care that goes unseen within families. Why are some forms of caring recognised as care, while others become almost invisible simply because they are considered part of family life?

I research trauma and adoption, and I am also an adoptive parent. I’m familiar with the story often told about adoption: a child finds a permanent family, a new life begins and everyone lives happily ever after.

But my research focuses on what happens after that supposed happy ending, particularly when the effects of a child’s earlier trauma continue into their adoptive family. And Burnham’s words made me wonder how much of the care provided by adoptive parents goes unrecognised simply because we call it parenting.
In England and Wales, an adoption order makes adopters the child’s legal parents. But a legal order cannot erase what happened beforehand.

Children adopted from care are often described as “previously looked-after”, a phrase I have long struggled with. There is nothing necessarily “previous” about the effects of their early experiences. A child may be physically safe but still struggle to feel safe. Earlier experiences can affect their development and their ability to trust the adults closest to them, since a family can be permanent in law long before a child feels secure enough to believe that permanence will last.

Adoptive parents are therefore living alongside the effects of experiences that happened before they even knew their child. This can make the parenting very different from what people usually imagine.

The relationship offering safety can also be the relationship in which fear and mistrust are expressed. For some families, this includes child-to-parent violence and abuse. A child experiencing overwhelming distress may run away or behave in ways that put themselves or others at risk. Parents may find themselves calling the police to protect their child or another family member, or because they fear for their own safety.

Understanding the reasons behind a child’s behaviour does not protect a parent from the emotional and physical impact of living with it. A parent can see why their child is hurting and still be hurt themselves.

My colleagues and I have researched compassion fatigue among adoptive parents raising children affected by early trauma. Compassion fatigue describes the emotional exhaustion and disconnection that can develop through repeated exposure to another person’s trauma.

My doctoral research also explored adoptive parents’ mental health more broadly. Parents described feeling exhausted while continuing to hold family life together. Sometimes, the very fact that they were managing made their distress harder for others to recognise.

The effects can reach beyond parents and children, affecting siblings and other family members. The adversity may belong to the child’s past, but its consequences can become part of the whole family’s present.
When families struggle to get help

Families are also affected by what happens outside the home. At school, a frightened child may be seen simply as badly behaved. A child who cannot get through the school gates may become an attendance problem. When the reasons behind their behaviour are overlooked, attention can quickly turn to what the parents are supposedly doing wrong.

Parents described fighting for help while feeling judged or blamed, sometimes until their family reached breaking point. Professionals, meanwhile, described recognising that families needed support but working within services that could not always provide it.

This is where Burnham’s description of a “threadbare system” particularly resonated with me. I have often described the services surrounding adoptive families as both traumatised and traumatising. Professionals are working under enormous pressure, often without the resources needed to respond to families’ complex needs. And when services are struggling, their responses can add to the distress of children and parents who are already finding life difficult.
For families, this can mean reaching a crisis and then having to demonstrate just how bad things have become before support is available.

Burnham’s words were powerful because they acknowledged care workers whose contribution is too often overlooked. But they also invite a wider conversation about what society recognises as care in the first place.

Care can come with a uniform and a job title. It can also mean a parent staying close to a child whose earliest relationships taught them that the adults they depend on may not always be safe or able to stay.
Helping a child learn to trust those relationships can take years, and the emotional demands on parents can be considerable. That work deserves recognition and support.
Care should not become less deserving of either simply because we call it parenting.

articles.title: DIY healthcare is on the rise – here’s why it’s so dangerous
articles.author: Dipa Kamdar, Associate Professor in Pharmacy Practice, Kingston University
paras: Need treatment fast? Many people now turn to Google before a healthcare professional. From checking symptoms online to buying medicines online and taking advice from social media influencers, healthcare is increasingly becoming a do-it-yourself activity.

Convenience is a big part of the appeal. Information is available instantly – no need to wait weeks to see a GP – and online communities often provide reassurance from people with similar experiences.

Researching a health problem on the internet can feel empowering. But while greater access to health information has benefits, the rise of DIY healthcare also comes with risks. Research suggests that diagnosing and treating yourself, or relying on unqualified sources for advice, can lead to mistakes, the wrong use of medicines and delays in getting professional help.

The internet has changed the way people access health information. A few decades ago, someone worried about a symptom might consult a doctor, pharmacist or medical reference book. Today, a search engine can generate thousands of results in seconds.
The problem is that not all health information online is reliable. Websites can be difficult to navigate, use complex language, or provide incomplete, outdated, or inaccurate information.
Social media platforms in particular play a major role in the rapid spread of inaccurate and misleading health information. This can make it hard for people to judge which sources they can trust.

Reliable sources generally explain the benefits and the risks, show the research their advice is based on, and admit when the evidence is uncertain. By contrast, advice that promises miracle cures, guarantees results or dismisses professional expertise should raise concerns.
Symptoms are often difficult to interpret without medical training. Headaches, fatigue, abdominal pain and skin rashes can have dozens of potential causes.

Searching for the term “headache” can bring up rare, frightening diagnoses such as brain tumours, causing needless panic. While online searches may occasionally point people in the right direction, they can also encourage unnecessary anxiety or false reassurance.

One of the most significant consequences of DIY healthcare is delayed access to professional support. Someone who is confident in an online diagnosis may postpone seeing a healthcare professional, even when symptoms persist or worsen. Early diagnosis often improves outcomes for conditions ranging from infections to cancer. When people spend weeks or months self-treating, opportunities for earlier intervention may be missed.
The trouble with influencers

The influence of social media extends beyond diagnosis. Increasingly, people are turning to influencers and content creators for treatment advice. Some recommend supplements, herbal remedies or over-the-counter medicines for everything from anxiety to chronic pain.

Unlike doctors and pharmacists, influencers don’t have to show that their advice is backed by research. Recommendations may be based on personal experience rather than scientific research. A treatment that appears harmless may interact with prescription medicines or worsen an existing condition.

For example, St John’s wort, a herbal remedy often taken for low mood, can make some prescription medicines work less well, including certain contraceptives and blood thinners. Without professional advice, these interactions can easily be missed.

Buying drugs online introduces further concerns. Thousands of websites now sell medicines directly to consumers, often promising convenience and privacy. While many online pharmacies operate legally, others do not.

The World Health Organization has repeatedly warned about counterfeit and substandard medicines entering global supply chains. These products may contain the wrong ingredients, incorrect doses or no active ingredient at all. They can fail to treat illness and, in some cases, cause direct harm.
Counterfeit medicines are particularly difficult for consumers to identify, especially when websites appear professional and trustworthy.

Taking an active role in your own care can help. People who understand their condition and join in treatment decisions are often better placed to manage it. But making your own decisions about your health works best when it is supported by reliable information and professional advice.
Three simple rules can help when you search for symptoms online.
Stick to trusted sources by relying on established medical institutions such as the NHS, rather than personal blogs or social media platforms.
Use the internet to prepare for an appointment: treat what you find as a list of questions for your doctor, and leave the diagnosis to them.

Treat online treatment advice with caution. A supplement, herbal remedy or medicine recommended by an influencer may not be supported by evidence and could interact with other treatments. When in doubt, check with a pharmacist or doctor before trying it.
Convenience and confidence don’t guarantee accuracy. Getting your health wrong can cost far more than the time you save.

articles.title: Cystic fibrosis patients got their ‘miracle drug’ thanks to federal research funding – new Trump administration rules may cut future miracles short
articles.author: Fred D. Ledley, Director, Center for Integration of Science and Industry, Bentley University
paras: The hardest disease to care for when I was training as a pediatrician in the late 1970s was cystic fibrosis, a disease in which abnormally thick mucus secretions block the lungs’ airways and make it progressively harder to breathe.

Back then, there was no treatment for the disease itself. All we had was physical therapy to clear mucus from the lungs, and drugs to dilate the airways and aid breathing. We used high doses of antibiotics to treat chronic pneumonia – drugs that also generated dangerous antibiotic-resistant infections that not only made the disease progressively harder to treat but also posed a threat to other people. At the same time, we also had to manage co-occurring conditions, including diabetes, malnutrition and heart failure.

Worse, these efforts did not work. In 1979 the median age of death from cystic fibrosis was 15. While all young deaths are tragic, caring for children with a progressive, inevitably fatal disease that denied emerging adolescents the promise of adulthood was especially heartbreaking.

Cystic fibrosis treatment changed dramatically after 2012, when the biotech company Vertex Pharmaceuticals launched the drug Kalydeco (ivacaftor), followed by additional cystic fibrosis drugs Orkambi (lumacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2015, Symdeko (tezacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2018, Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2019 and Alyftrek (vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor) in 2024.

Now, the median survival age for a child with cystic fibrosis born today in the United States is 66 years. Mary Vought, the former wife of the director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, stated that their daughter, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, “can live likely a full life because of this miracle drug,” and that “it is very, very, very hopeful.”

Cystic fibrosis treatments are not miracles; they required decades of research funded by a combination of public and private investments. The largest contributor to this work was the National Institutes of Health, which funded much of the pivotal research required to understand the genetics and biology of the disease. Only with this knowledge was it possible to begin searching for drugs to treat cystic fibrosis.

Ironically, the federal funding that was so critical to developing these drugs is now threatened by policies that were initially proposed by the Office of Management and Budget. Those policies, which would increase political control over federal research grants, limit peer review and curtail research on certain topics, were temporarily blocked by Congress. But several federal agencies are still pursing portions of this agenda, including the NIH.
NIH laid the foundation for treatment

My colleagues and I examined the role that federal funding from the National Institutes of Health has played in developing cystic fibrosis treatments. We found that NIH funding supported more than 6,200 published research papers on the biology of cystic fibrosis in the 27 years before Kalydeco was approved in 2012.

Some of these publications describe celebrated milestones in understanding the biology of CFTR – the gene that causes cystic fibrosis – or the disease process. Others describe the studies necessary to replicate, refute or refine these advances and ensure the necessary scientific rigor to successfully discover and develop new drugs.

Overall, we identified US$3.2 billion in NIH funding for basic research on cystic fibrosis from 1985 to 2012 and approximately $940 million in funding for applied research on potential drugs. This funding complemented at least $200 million in investments from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation for the discovery or development of these drugs as well as undisclosed spending by Vertex to develop and commercialize these products.

The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation acknowledged the essential role of the NIH in a 2025 letter to Russell Vought and other Trump administration leaders, writing that “ensuring that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) is fully functional is critical for furthering our knowledge of the biology of CF and advancing CF therapeutic development.”
What will it take to produce future miracles?
Developing groundbreaking drugs requires a long-term, sustained commitment from the public, from the government and from industry.

FDA-approved drugs are typically based on 20 to 30 years of basic research in the lab and eight to nine years of human testing in the clinic. This work is supported, at least in part, by an average of $1.4 billion in NIH funding and as much as a reported $1.4 billion in industry funding per drug.

Russell Vought and his family have benefited from the commitment that scientists, advocates, legislators and industry leaders have placed into developing treatments that now offer patients with cystic fibrosis a normal life. A similar commitment can help find cures for patients who don’t respond to available drugs and to provide cures for cardiovascular disease, cancer, dementia and other conditions.

This commitment to research is currently under threat from Trump administration proposals that would reduce NIH funding, research, training and global research collaboration. Protecting or expanding federal funding for basic research instead can help lead to innovative therapies for countless patients.

articles.title: I’m a pediatrician and a mom - here’s how to treat lice without stigma
articles.author: Emily J. C. Wong, Associate Professor of Pediatrics, University of Virginia
paras: Four words that parents in the classroom group chat dread to read: ‘My kid has lice.’

Head lice (Pediculus humanus capitis) are parasites that primarily infest children in childcare, preschool or elementary school. Having lice doesn’t indicate poor hygiene, despite a longstanding misconception driven by stigma, and lice don’t spread other diseases. But children with lice are often shamed and unnecessarily excluded from attending school.

As a primary care pediatrician with specialized training in infections and infestations of microbes, viruses and tiny pests such as lice, my goal is to keep children healthy so that they can stay in school. And as a mother of two, I personally have experienced the battle against lice with my own children.

Head lice have been humans’ unwanted companions since ancient times. Understanding how they spread, as well as how to detect and treat infestations, can help parents and schools handle head lice effectively without fear.

Adult head lice are gray-tan insects with six legs, approximately 2-3 millimeters long – about the size of a sesame seed. They live exclusively on humans, feeding on blood by biting the scalp and using their saliva to prevent the blood from coagulating.
Female lice lay eggs on hair close to the scalp, attaching the eggs firmly to the hair shaft with a secreted glue-like substance. The eggs take 8 to 9 days to hatch.

Since head lice cannot jump or fly, they most often spread from person to person through direct head-to-head contact. In school, this might happen when children are sitting very close to each other or napping alongside classmates. Eggs or lice can also be spread when kids share objects like hats or hair brushes, but this route is much less common because they don’t live long off of the head.
There is no medical evidence that certain types of hair are resistant. Lice can infest all hair types.

Your child might have lice if you see them frequently scratching their scalp. That itchiness is a sensitivity reaction most children develop to lice saliva. It can take four to six weeks for the sensitization to develop in children who have never had lice before – which means your child has likely had lice for a few weeks by the time you discover them.
What to do if you think your child has head lice
First of all, don’t panic. A head lice infestation can be frustrating or embarrassing, but it’s not dangerous and there are effective treatments.

Look closely at your child’s scalp for live lice. They move fast and avoid light, so it might be difficult to find one. Be sure to check for eggs, which are often behind the ears or at the nape of the neck. Eggs are securely attached to hair and not flaky like dandruff.

Once you are sure your child has head lice, check other household members, too. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that you treat all household members who have lice, as well as anyone who shares a bed with the child, even if you don’t find lice or eggs on them.
Several treatment options exist that are approved by the Food and Drug Administration, safe for children, available over the counter and affordable:

1% permethrin is available as a lotion or a cream rinse and sold under the brand name Nix in the U.S. as well as in generic forms. It can be used for children 2 months and older. It kills live lice effectively but not eggs, so you’ll need to reapply it in nine to 10 days to kill any lice that may have hatched since the first treatment.

Pyrethrins + piperonyl butoxide shampoo is sold under the brand name Rid and in generic form. This substance can be used for children 24 months and older. Like 1% permethrin, it generally needs to be reapplied nine to 10 days after first use.

Ivermectin 0.5% lotion can be used for kids older than 6 months. In addition to killing adult lice, ivermectin continues to kill new lice that hatch after treatment, so a single application should do the job.

After the topical treatment, comb the hair with a fine-toothed comb to ensure that no live lice remain. Using a creamy conditioner as you comb can make lice more visible. Since no treatment is 100% effective, combing also helps to remove eggs that would later hatch into live lice and would need to be killed with the second treatment. Getting rid of the empty nits isn’t necessary, but it can reduce a child’s embarrassment and parental worry.
What if treatment doesn’t work?

An itchy head after topical treatment may just be a reaction to the treatment itself. Check for live lice or new eggs, which would be sitting within 1-2 millimeters of the hair base, rather than empty nits that are whiter and farther along the hair shaft.

Sometimes over-the-counter treatments don’t work fully – either due to user error or re-exposure, or because the lice have developed a resistance to them. If you have the resources, lice removal salons or clinics – available in most urban and suburban areas – can offer professional help. Alternatively, you should be able to get one of these second-line therapies, available by prescription only, from your child’s healthcare provider:

Malathion 0.5% lotion is sold as brand-name Ovide or as a generic form and approved for children age 6 and older. Because malathion is highly flammable, you cannot expose the treated hair to any heat, even a hair dryer. If you see live lice in seven to nine days, repeat the treatment.
Spinosad 0.9% suspension is available as the brand-name Natroba or as a generic liquid. You can apply it on children 6 months and older. Repeat the treatment if you see live lice in seven days.

Ivermectin oral tablets are approved to treat lice in adults, but not in children. However, since oral ivermectin is approved in children for other parasitic infections who weigh at least 33 lbs, doctors can use it to treat lice off-label.

If you would prefer to avoid chemical treatment, you can try manually removing every single louse and using an emollient with dimethicone lotion. However, research on whether this technique is effective is limited. And none of the many alternative remedies for treating lice – such as smothering them with mayonnaise or oil, dehydrating them with saline or hot air, or zapping them with an electronic comb – have proven to be effective.

Lice do not survive more than 48 hours off the head. To kill lice or eggs that have jumped to surfaces, wash all clothing, bedding, head wear and toys that came in contact with the child’s head in the past two days in hot water and dry them on high heat. Vacuum furniture and carpets to remove hair, and place any objects that cannot be washed in plastic bags for two weeks.
What about school attendance?

Beginning in the 1980’s, as an effort to contain outbreaks of head lice, many schools in the United States adopted “No Nit” policies that excluded children from attendance if any eggs or empty nits were found on the child’s head.

However, many medical experts and public health organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, reject these policies as unnecessary and ineffective. Keeping children out of school due to lice also contributes to social stigma.

According to current guidelines, if a child has a head lice infestation, they should not be sent home early from school. Instead, the school should notify parents, and the child should keep attending school as they are being treated. They should also avoid close head contact and sharing items like hats, scarves and hairbrushes.
Some schools continue to check students’ hair for nits after treatment, but this practice is not effective since empty nits without live lice can persist in hair for weeks or even months.
Emily J. Wong is affiliated with the American Academy of Pediatrics. She receives funding from the American Academy of Pediatrics.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer highlights growing number of nonsmokers diagnosed with the disease – and younger people too
articles.author: Estelamari Rodriguez, Associate Director of Community Outreach in Thoracic Oncology, University of Miami
paras: When many people think of an average lung cancer patient, they often imagine an older man smoking. But the face of lung cancer has changed. Over the past 15 years, more women, never smokers and younger people are being diagnosed with lung cancer.

In fact, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death among women, and more women die from lung cancer than breast, ovarian and colorectal cancer each year. The American Lung Association reports that while lung cancer rates have risen by 79% for women over the last 44 years, they decreased by 43% for men. And for the first time in history, there are more young women than men diagnosed with lung cancer.

News about Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer diagnosis on Oct. 13, 2026, sparked discussion about increasing rates of the disease among people who have never smoked. Leo reportedly is not a smoker. Potential causes for the disease include environmental exposures and genetics, and recognizing the diverse factors that can increase someone’s risk of lung cancer – regardless of their smoking history – is essential for timely and appropriate screening and treatment.

Cancer that is found at the earliest stages, like that of the pope, can be treated with surgery and cured for both smokers and nonsmokers. The challenge is that people who have never smoked are not currently included in lung cancer screening guidelines, and tumors are often only found by chance.

As a thoracic oncologist, I have seen many younger women and never smokers walk into my clinic with a new diagnosis of lung cancer. Particularly for never smokers, lung cancer is unexpected for both patients and their doctors, which can often lead to delays in diagnosis. Researchers have described this trend of increasing lung cancer rates among women in different parts of the world and are starting to understand why cases are on the rise.
The first explanation of why rates of lung cancer in women have increased is that many started smoking later than men, pushing back their peak in smoking-related lung cancer diagnoses.

Women also started smoking in the years when filtered cigarettes were most commonly used. This led to an increased risk of a type of cancer called adenocarcinoma due to the way cigarette filters distribute tobacco smoke to the outer parts of the lungs. Some studies suggest that women are more susceptible to the carcinogenic effects of exposure to tobacco and cigarette smoke, including second-hand smoke, and may develop lung cancer after fewer years of smoking compared to men.

However, it is important to note that most people diagnosed today with lung cancer are not active smokers. About 20% of women with lung cancer have never smoked – higher than for men with lung cancer who’ve never smoked.
Besides smoking and secondhand smoke, there are several other lung cancer risk factors. These include a family history of cancer and exposure to asbestos, radon and air pollution.

Exposure to carcinogens in the workplace in the form of inhaled chemicals such as arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, silica and nickel is still a concern in some parts of the world. The potential lung cancer risk of e-cigarette and marijuana smoke is still under study but of potential concern.

Recently, researchers have also found that genetics can play a role in lung cancer risk in some patients with a strong history of lung cancer. Studies of these families have helped identify potential susceptibility genes for lung cancer and environmental risk factors.

Like BRCA1 and BRCA2 in breast cancer, alterations in genes that promote or protect against tumor development can contribute to lung cancer development. Researchers have yet to identify specific mutations that may predispose individuals to lung cancer. However, studying familial genetic predispositions can help elucidate how lung cancer develops and lead to new biomarkers for early cancer detection in high-risk groups.

In 2021, the United States Preventive Services Task Force updated its lung cancer screening guidelines to include younger patients with less smoking history. Now, lung cancer screening is recommended for adults ages 50 to 80 who have smoked at least one pack per day for 20 years, current smokers and former smokers who quit smoking within the last 15 years. Women at risk for lung cancer can talk to their doctors about ordering a low-dose CT scan for lung cancer screening.

Nationwide, more than 70% of eligible women undergo breast cancer screening but less than 6% of all eligible smokers pursue lung cancer screening. Researchers estimate that these new screening guidelines will increase the number of women eligible for lung cancer screening by 40% by including those at a younger age who have less smoking exposure.

In recent years, increasing understanding of the genetic changes that can lead to cancer and how to harness the immune system to treat cancer has led to new targeted therapies and immunotherapies that have improved the prognosis of patients with lung cancer. Women tend to have a better lung cancer prognosis than men, especially if they never smoked and have tumors with molecular changes that can be treated with targeted therapies.

However, lung cancer symptoms may go unrecognized in women. Symptoms of lung cancer can include coughing, shortness of breath, overwhelming fatigue and pain in the back, chest or shoulder, which could be confused for other ailments. Because women tend to be slightly younger when diagnosed than men, patients may be able to tolerate symptoms longer and delay seeking medical attention. Physicians also might not attribute these symptoms to lung cancer due to a patient’s younger age.

Recognizing the early symptoms of lung cancer, expanding lung cancer screening eligibility and testing for genetic biomarkers to select the best therapy are some of the steps that could help address the global epidemic of lung cancer in women.
This is an updated version of an article published on Feb. 1, 2023.

articles.title: Doing a short cardio session after weight training probably won’t boost your gains – here’s why
articles.author: Liam T. Pearson-Noseworthy, Distinguished Teaching Fellow, School of Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation, Northumbria University, Newcastle
paras: Spend long enough on fitness social media and you’ll see the same tip. Finish every weight training session with about 15 minutes of cardio to boost your “gains”. But does it actually work? Probably not as much as you’d think.
Doing cardio and weight training in the same exercise programme is known as “concurrent training”. This includes doing cardio in the same session as your weights, or on separate days.

For years, people thought concurrent training held back strength and muscle gains. This worry goes back to 1980 when a ten-week study found that people who did both on the same days, within two hours of each other, built less strength than those who only lifted.

This became known as the “interference effect”: the idea that cardio gets in the way of building muscle and strength. And there’s some logic to keeping cardio short. A 2012 review found that the longer and more often people did cardio alongside their lifting, the more it ate into their strength, muscle and power gains. That puts a 15-minute bout at the low-risk end.
But research has come a long way since 1980, and now shows the interference effect may not be as significant as once thought.
A major 2022 review pooled 43 studies involving 1,090 people. It compared people who did cardio alongside a weights programme against people who only did the weights programme.
Adding cardio made no real difference to how much muscle people built or how much stronger they got. That held whether the cardio was cycling or running.
A 2026 review of 17 earlier analyses covering 144 studies reached the same conclusion. It also found that adding cardio improved aerobic fitness without costing strength, power or muscle.

This research clearly shows that a cardio finisher isn’t going to wreck progress. But it’s also worth noting that this research didn’t suggest adding cardio made muscle or strength gains any bigger. On average, people who did cardio and weights gained similar muscle and strength to those who only lifted, though there are two exceptions to this finding.

The first is explosive strength, the kind you use to jump or sprint. This improved slightly less when people added cardio. But that dip only showed up when cardio and weights were done within 20 minutes of each other. When the two were at least three hours apart, it wasn’t there. A finisher done straight after lifting falls inside that window.

The second is experience. Across 27 studies, adding cardio held back leg strength gains in experienced gym-goers – but only when both were done in the same session. Beginners saw no clear difference. The 2026 review points out that there’s very little research on elite athletes, though, and they’re the people most likely to notice even a small dip in performance.
There’s also an early hint that adding cardio could affect the muscle fibres themselves. These are the individual cells that make up a muscle.

A review of 15 studies found that adding cardio to a weights programme may slightly reduce muscle fibre growth. This effect may be more pronounced with running than cycling – at least in one type of muscle fibre. But the authors were careful to call this research preliminary, and it didn’t show up when whole muscles were measured.

If you’re doing both weight training and cardio in one session, lift first. A review from Northumbria University found lifting before cardio provided about 7% greater gains in lower-body strength than the other way round.
A second review found the same pattern. But when it came to aerobic fitness, neither review found the order made any difference.
However, I couldn’t find any studies testing a 15-minute finisher head-on against separate cardio sessions. And the studies that are out there, on average, were judged to be of medium quality.

It’s also worth doing the maths: three 15-minute finishers a week adds up to 45 minutes. The UK’s chief medical officers recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus strength work on at least two days.

That gap matters. High aerobic fitness is linked to about half the risk of early death compared with low fitness. Doing both strength and aerobic exercise is linked to a 40% lower risk of early death than doing neither.
How much you do matters too. Even 75 minutes of moderate activity a week is linked to a 23% lower risk of early death compared with doing none – with the biggest gains up to around 150 minutes.
What about fat loss, the other big selling point of the cardio finisher?

A 2025 review of 36 studies found that people who added cardio to their weight training programme lost about 1kg more fat than those who only lifted – but only in studies lasting ten weeks or more. That gap also disappeared in studies where both groups trained for the same length of time or burned roughly the same calories. Same-day or separate-day cardio made no difference.

The bottom line is that if you enjoy doing your cardio after a weight training session, then you should keep doing it. A short finisher won’t hurt your gains, and it works your heart and lungs in ways you might not otherwise with weight training alone.

If muscle size is your main goal, a bike may be a slightly safer bet than a treadmill. Running, but not cycling, has been linked to smaller gains in muscle size and strength – though the evidence is still thin.

If power is your priority, or you’re an experienced lifter chasing a personal best, give cardio its own session a few hours later if possible. Just don’t treat a finisher as a shortcut to bigger or stronger “gains”, or as your cardio done for the week. It’s a good start, not the whole job.

articles.title: A drug can make children with the most common form of dwarfism taller – but height isn’t the same as a better life
articles.author: Erin Pritchard, Senior lecturer in Disability Studies, Liverpool Hope University
paras: A drug that helps children with the most common form of dwarfism grow taller has sparked an ethical debate within the dwarfism community.

Some parents hope that as well as increasing size, it will prevent serious health complications and improve their children’s independence. But critics worry that a treatment focused on increasing height sends the message that dwarfism is something that needs to be corrected.

The drug, vosoritide, sold as Voxzogo, is used to treat children with achondroplasia, a genetic condition that restricts bone growth. It works by reducing the activity of a signal that slows bone growth. Approved in Europe in 2021, it is now authorised for children from four months old while their bones are still growing.
Clinical trials show that vosoritide increases growth. But whether it can prevent serious medical complications or improve quality of life in the longer term remains uncertain.
This raises difficult questions about what constitutes a successful treatment and how much say people with achondroplasia should have in deciding what those outcomes should be.
Growth rate measures bones, not lives

The evidence that vosoritide increases growth is now well established. Longer-term trial data show that children receiving the drug continue to grow faster than untreated children with achondroplasia over several years.

Parents may hope that treatment will also reduce some of the medical complications associated with achondroplasia, such as spinal stenosis, where narrowing of the spinal canal can put pressure on nerves, or improve independence later in life.

There is some encouraging early evidence. A 2026 trial found preliminary signs that early vosoritide treatment may improve spinal development. Another study found lower rates of some complications among children in vosoritide trials compared with published data about people who had not received the drug.
These findings are promising, but they do not yet establish whether treatment will prevent serious complications throughout life.

The spinal study followed children for only one year and included relatively small numbers, particularly when participants were divided into different age groups. Small studies make it harder to determine whether differences represent genuine treatment effects, especially for uncommon complications.

The second study included 230 children who received vosoritide, but compared their outcomes with previously published data rather than randomly assigning children to treated and untreated groups. Differences between these populations may have influenced the results.

There are also reasons for caution about assuming that starting treatment very early will prevent serious complications. Two infants who began vosoritide within days of birth still developed progressive foramen magnum stenosis, a narrowing at the base of the skull that can compress the brainstem and spinal cord. Both required surgery.

A report involving two children cannot establish how commonly this happens or whether vosoritide altered their risk. However, it demonstrates that early treatment does not necessarily prevent these complications.
What does a better quality of life mean?
Improving quality of life is another potential benefit of treatment, although measuring it is complicated.

Research involving people with achondroplasia has found that they can experience difficulties relating to health and physical functioning, alongside social barriers associated with living in a world designed around average-height bodies.

If quality-of-life measures include difficulty accessing buildings or experiences of discrimination, these problems cannot automatically be solved by changing a child’s body. Treatment may help some children manage everyday activities, but accessible environments and reduced discrimination are also needed.

The experience of receiving treatment deserves attention too. Vosoritide requires daily injections throughout the growing years. Research with seven families of children aged two to four found that injections could involve fear, pain and distress, although experiences varied.

These questions are especially relevant given the history of treatments intended to increase height. Limb-lengthening surgery, for example, remains contentious. A 2026 systematic review found that it can produce substantial increases in limb length, but involves prolonged treatment and carries a high risk of complications.
Decisions about such interventions have long raised questions about when children can meaningfully participate in choosing treatments that may affect them for years.
Who should decide what successful treatment looks like?

Adults with achondroplasia have been included in some research, and international guidance published in 2025 included two patient representatives. However, much of the evidence informing treatment decisions still comes from clinical trials and assessments made by clinicians and parents.

The guidance was financially supported by BioMarin, the manufacturer of vosoritide, and participants received honoraria for their involvement in the consensus process. The authors state that BioMarin did not influence the recommendations.

About 80% of people with achondroplasia are born to parents of average height. This makes the experiences of adults living with the condition particularly valuable when families are considering treatment.
Parents routinely make healthcare decisions for children who are too young to consent. They need clear information that distinguishes established benefits from hoped-for or still uncertain outcomes.

As children grow, their views should increasingly be included in decisions about their treatment. Current international guidance recommends that young people should have opportunities to agree to treatment, raise concerns or express disagreement. It also recommends that families are informed about the uncertainties surrounding long-term outcomes.

The ethical debate surrounding vosoritide therefore extends beyond whether the drug makes children taller. It also concerns which health benefits have been demonstrated, how treatment affects children day to day and who gets to define success.

Adults with achondroplasia have knowledge that clinical measurements cannot provide. Their experiences should help shape the outcomes researchers study and the information families receive when deciding whether treatment is right for their child.
